subsubtopic: CALL FOR REVERSAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a constituent in my riding of Erie, who has invested in the lift truck sales and services business, has once again written to me concerning the rising prime interest rates. His letter reads in part, "The government apparently really does not want to help the small businessmen survive this terrible crisis in which they find themselves." In light of the desperation that lies behind these words of my constituent, words which are being repeated all over Canada, I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid):
That the government reverse its policy of "state intervention" and "government ownership", and introduce policies to restore investor confidence in the Canadian private sector.

subsubtopic: SIZE OF GOVERNMENT DEFICIT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. It is no surprise that last week business leaders supported the government's position on wage restraint in the public sector. It was also clear, as a result of those meetings and arising out of those meetings, that they in no way supported the other elements of the recent federal government budget. In fact they expressed shock at the size of the federal government deficit. They indicated that their greatest single disappointment was the fact that nothing had been done to change the National Energy Program in a fundamental way. What action is the Prime Minister planning to take to respond to these deeply held concerns of the business community leaders? In particular, what action is he proposing to take to reduce the size of the federal government deficit and to reduce the size of the increase in government spending which this year will have a second consecutive increase of 20 per cent?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: SIZE OF GOVERNMENT DEFICIT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am somewhat puzzled at the report that the hon. member has been given of that meeting. It is true that some of the participants expressed surprise at the size of the deficit, but others pointed out to them that they should not have been surprised if they had looked at the slowdown in the economy and had done their calculations. Some of the participants, and indeed some of the premiers the week before, indicated that they had anticipated a deficit of that size basing it on their own deficits which had almost doubled from one year to the next.
If my memory is correct, just a few weeks before the budget the hon. member was predicting a deficit of something between $16 billion and $20 billion. Therefore, why would he now think they were surprised unless they had been very much misinformed?

Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister has again totally ignored the question that I asked him. I asked him what he was proposing to do to reduce the size of the federal government deficit which is keeping upward pressure on interest rates, and in the words of the Minister of Finance, high deficits and high increases in government spending, running at 20 per cent per annum two years running, will increase inflation and increase the level of interest rates. What is he going to do to meet those concerns?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member is arguing economic policy. The answer to his question was given by the Minister of Finance, that this deficit is one which is essentially due to the automatic stabilizers. It is due to the fact that the economy has slowed down, as everyone knows. Therefore, the revenues of the government on one hand have been reduced, and its expenditures have been increased in order once again to pay for the automatic stabilizers. Therefore, as the Minister of Finance has indicated, and I have not heard the hon. member gainsay it yet, when the economy recovers, this deficit will be automatically reduced.
It is not a deficit which is planned, such as in other countries which are cutting their taxes and increasing their expenses. It is a deficit which came in spite of the fact that we did not increase our expenditures in any substantive way.

subtopic: REPORT OF PROJECTED INCREASE IN DEFICIT
REPORT OF PROJECTED INCREASE IN DEFICIT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister is dealing in probably the worst flim-flam we have heard in the House in months. The government is increasing its spending by 20 per cent. That was the shock to business people. They thought there would be a program of restraint in the face of the size of the government deficit, which is bound to increase interest rates. They were also surprised that again the government increased taxes-in the second budget in the row-at a time of deep recession in the country, which is bound to deepen that recession further and therefore increase the size of the budget deficit.
What is the government going to do about the size of the budget deficit? Last week Maclean's magazine reported the projection of Department of Finance officials that the budget deficit would be $22 billion next year. What is the government going to do to reduce that deficit?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REPORT OF PROJECTED INCREASE IN DEFICIT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member would like me to repeat my previous answer. I answered him about our approach to the deficit. He talks about increased government expenditures. I point out to him that it is true that in the last budget expenditures of some $2.3 billion were forecast for this year and next year in order to create direct jobs and in order to increase assistance to housing, small businesses, fishermen, farmers and others. It is true that such expenditures were announced in the budget.
July 12, 1982

However, if the hon. member looks at the other side of the budget, he will see that that money is not increasing the deficit. As the hon. member himself says, there is a redistributive effect, and that money is the result.

subtopic: REPORT OF PROJECTED INCREASE IN DEFICIT
speechtext: Cutting old age pensions.

subtopic: REPORT OF PROJECTED INCREASE IN DEFICIT
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition wants to get into this. I hope, Madam Speaker, you will recognize him before three o'clock, because we generally do not see him before three o'clock.
The reasoning behind the budget is not a Conservative reasoning. That is why hon. members opposite do not understand it. What we are doing is saying to those who have jobs, security and incomes, that they should share with those who do not have jobs, security and incomes. That is the philosophy behind the budget, and Canadians are open to that kind of thinking, even though it is foreign to the Tory Party.

subtopic: REPORT OF PROJECTED INCREASE IN DEFICIT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, my question is also directed to the Prime Minister. The question really is what proportion of the economy of the country the government is taking, and it is clear the government is taking an increasing share at the expense of all Canadians, pensioners included.
The Prime Minister has indicated he would like Canadians voluntarily to follow the wage control program he has imposed on employees within the federal jurisdiction. In answer to a question during a news conference following the first ministers' meeting several weeks ago, he indicated he did not have the power to impose general controls except in the event that, and 1 quote:
-we would have to use our emergency powers and in order to have those emergency powers stick in front of the courts there has to be a recognized emergency.
Would the Prime Minister classify a failure by his government to achieve the co-operation of the provinces and the business and labour sectors as a failure which constitutes a national emergency?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member prefaced his question by indicating that the federal government was increasing its share of the gross national product by its spending. I point out to him that the share spent by the government directly on goods and services has fallen slightly over the past ten years. What has increased enormously is transfers to the provinces and, of course, service of the public debt. Perhaps the hon. member would like to refer to those statistics before misleading himself into believing that the federal government is suddenly occupying a larger part of the economic spectrum. It is not.
As to the question about recognizing an emergency, the hon. member knows the Constitution. He knows the judgment of the Supreme Court on the price and wage control program adopted in 1975. He will recall that that decision was that it is only in a national emergency that the federal government is
Oral Questions
constitutionally able to impose over-all wage and price controls. The definition of that emergency, according to some judges, depended very much on the attitude of the provinces. If the provinces themselves are not in any sense urging the federal government to use those powers, what I indicated at the press conference and in this House in response to the Leader of the New Democratic Party, is that it would probably be quite difficult to make it stick in the courts.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is also for the Prime Minister. In 1974 when the Prime Minister felt there was a national emergency, interest rates were about 11 per cent, the inflation rate was about 11 per cent, the national deficit was about $1.6 billion, and 514,000 people were unemployed. Today interest rates and the prime rate are around 18 per cent, the inflation rate is around 11 per cent, the national debt is $20 billion, and 1,300,000 people are unemployed. And there is a liquidity crisis today in business. During all but nine months of the last eight years the Prime Minister has been the leader of this country. Would he tell the House what his bottom line is for economic indicators before he considers that there is an emergency? What are his options, except for the complete control of the Canadian economy?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, after arguing that there is a kind of emergency that would justify complete controls, the hon. member then asks what my options are except complete controls. I think he is like certain chickens that lay beautiful eggs, but then turn around and eat them. He should review his question.
I am not sure if he is arguing for controls or if he is arguing that there is a kind of emergency now which gives us constitutional power to impose controls. If it is the latter, then I would refer him to my previous answer and to the fact that in 1975 when this Parliament adopted over-all price and wage controls there had been two meetings of the premiers in August, 1974, and August, 1975, when they had urged the federal government to take its responsibility to bring inflation down. They have not done that in the recent meetings or in recent public statements. Perhaps they will at their August meeting; I do not know. They have not taken that point of view to date. That is the difference between 1975 and 1982.

subsubtopic: MORTGAGE REDUCTION SCHEME
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister which concerns a new confusion in government policy which affects both would-be home owners and the building industry. In his budget speech

July 12, 1982
Oral Questions
the Minister of Finance announced the appointment of a blue ribbon committee which would examine the feasibility of a mortgage reduction scheme which, to use his words, if implemented would bring down mortgages by 3 to 6 per cent. On the weekend the minister responsible for housing took an entirely different approach. He said categorically that there would be such a scheme. In fact he urged Canadians to buy new homes now.
Will the Prime Minister clear up this confusion? Is the government certain that it will proceed with the 3 to 6 per cent mortgage reduction scheme, or is it still up in the air?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: MORTGAGE REDUCTION SCHEME
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have not read the speech of the hon. minister responsible for housing but, knowing him as I do, I suspect the confusion is probably in the questioner rather than in the minister. The Leader of the New Democratic Party knows that the new credit instrument the minister talked about is only to be reported on some time in late September. Consideration of implementing it would follow that. That is known to every minister and every member of the House, and certainly to the minister responsible for housing. The Minister of Finance brought in bridging financing which would make it profitable for people to buy a house now rather than wait for the report of the blue ribbon committee.
The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition shakes his head negatively, Madam Speaker. He is misinformed. The Minister of Finance announced a $3,000 grant for first-time home buyers or buyers of new homes. That is available now. The other measure, if implemented, would presumably take place much later this year.

subsubtopic: MORTGAGE REDUCTION SCHEME
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I say to the Prime Minister that it is he who is confused in his facts, not I.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR GUARANTEE TO HOME PURCHASERS
REQUEST FOR GUARANTEE TO HOME PURCHASERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is important in light of what the minister responsible for housing said on television last night to the people of the country, when he urged them to go out and buy a home now. He was talking about the mortgage reduction scheme, not the $3,000 grant in this instance.
A difference of between 3 per cent to 6 per cent in the price of a home, as the Prime Minister should know, could mean hundreds of dollars per month in terms of payments. Therefore I should like the Prime Minister to speak in terms of government policy now. Is the government committed in principle to the scheme which will reduce mortgages by 3 per cent to 6 per cent, in line with what the minister told people in the country to do yesterday-to go out and buy on that assumption? If so, is he, as Prime Minister, prepared to guarantee to home purchasers that their mortgages will come down by 3 per cent to 6 per cent?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR GUARANTEE TO HOME PURCHASERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member calculated quickly that 3 per cent to 6 per cent would mean hundreds of dollars per month. Well, if he calculates quickly he will find that a couple of hundred dollars per month is something like $3,000.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR GUARANTEE TO HOME PURCHASERS
speechtext: Oh, come on!

subtopic: REQUEST FOR GUARANTEE TO HOME PURCHASERS
speechtext: You have never had a mortgage, I can tell you that.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR GUARANTEE TO HOME PURCHASERS
speechtext: They have not found that over there. The $3,000, it is stated quite clearly in the budget, is something which goes into effect here and now.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR GUARANTEE TO HOME PURCHASERS
speechtext: It is a one-time payment.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR GUARANTEE TO HOME PURCHASERS
speechtext:
Yes, it is a one-time payment, because the expectation is that the other measure will be recommended and implemented. But until it is, the House can give no guarantee.
The minister deliberately set up a consultative mechanism partially in response to the criticism after the November budget that he had not consulted enough. In this particular case he set up this mechanism to ensure that he would have the support of the financial community and of other interested parties. But, in the meantime, he gave this offer of a one-time $3,000 grant. The two are distinct, but both are meant to help home owners.

Madam Speaker, I ask the Prime Minister to listen with care to the question. There are two different schemes. The Prime Minister is talking about one. I am talking about the one the minister discussed on television last night and discussed in an interview with The Toronto Star, namely, the mortgage reduction scheme. In Saturday's Toronto Star the minister is quoted as saying, "There is no question of chance. The plan will be implemented. The government is committed to it". That scheme is the mortgage reduction scheme. Will the Prime Minister, and therefore the government, not simply the minister, guarantee to Canadians who purchase homes now that they will benefit from the 3 per cent to 6 per cent reduction mortgage scheme which the minister promised?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member is again referring to a speech which I have not read or heard. Therefore, what 1 answered in response to the first question is subject to me verifying it. But the hon. member knows that I could not give the guarantee which he is seeking. I do not think the minister himself would have given it.
He did on television last night.

Certainly it is the hope and the policy of government that it will be found acceptable and that it will be
July 12, 1982

implemented. If this is what the minister was saying, certainly he was stating government policy. But if it was a guarantee that such and such a project will be adopted by this blue ribbon committee and then voted by the House, the hon. member is presuming on both the decision of the committee and on the decision of the House, which I know he would not do.
That is what Cosgrove did.

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE FUTURE CUTBACKS-REQUEST FOR COMMITMENT TO PUBLIC HEARINGS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. Undoubtedly he has now had time to have perused the very comprehensive and constructive Senate report on the unilateral action of the minister last year to cut VIA Rail by 20 per cent. Since we are in the summer period again, would the minister give an unequivocal assurance and commitment to the House, following along recommendation No. 2 of the Senate report, that there will be no further cutbacks to VIA Rail operations or rail line abandonments unless and until the public forum route is followed?

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE FUTURE CUTBACKS-REQUEST FOR COMMITMENT TO PUBLIC HEARINGS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, strangely enough the negative aspects of the Senate report have been emphasized, but I would say that I agree with 75 per cent of what the Senate report indicates. When it talks about fixed costs, for example, I would agree. When it talks about the need for legislation, I agree. It is really on the assessment of the capacity of the government to increase the subsidies going to VIA that the agreement between the Senate and myself breaks down. I simply do not think that it is possible for the government to go on adding to those subsidies until they reach $1 billion or more. That is why the government took the action that it took last year. I am also a bit surprised that the Senate report seems to imply that I was acting illegally when I took that action, as it was taken under Section 64 of the National Transportation Act. With respect to future cuts, I can say very simply that this is not the intention of the government at this time.

Madam Speaker, coming to the last part of the answer in terms of future cuts at this time, we are talking possibly of another summer, or autumn, adjournment, whenever the House adjourns. Can the minister not give an assurance that there will be no cuts until the public forum route is followed?
I will not get into a debate on the substance of subsidies. Obviously if subsidies have to be paid out and the traffic is not there, one has to be responsible and to take action after a public discussion. That was part of the central theme of the
Oral Questions
Senate report, it being critical of the minister being able to discontinue unilaterally the passenger train service of the country. Perhaps that is the minister's wish; 1 do not know.
If the minister cannot give an assurance about any future cuts regardless of public discussion, when will the minister bring in the VIA Rail act and/or the discussion paper which he said would precede the VIA Rail act? Could we at least have that on the Table of the House before we get out of here?

Madam Speaker, I already said to the Standing Committee on Transport that 1 would be submitting a VIA paper. I was hoping to do so during the summer, but I can assure the hon. member that it will be there awaiting him to study it in committee in the fall. That is on the first point.
On the second point, I can only repeat that the National Transportation Act under Section 64 gives the government the right to do what it did. There are circumstances when it can be justified. I explained myself 100 times on that subject last summer. I cannot say that Section 64 of the National Transportation Act will never be used. I can only say, as I did a moment ago, that this is not the intention of government at this time.

subtopic: QUERY RESPECTING THE HOLDING OF PUBLIC HEARINGS
QUERY RESPECTING THE HOLDING OF PUBLIC HEARINGS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the same minister. It flows out of the conversations, press releases and press stories over the past two or three days. Is the minister leading the House to believe that he has no intention of going to the public hearing process before termination of VIA Rail services in the future, or is the minister agreeing with the all-party Senate report that there should be public hearings before the implementation of future rail cuts?

subtopic: QUERY RESPECTING THE HOLDING OF PUBLIC HEARINGS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have already indicated my intention, the intention of the government, but under the law it is possible for government to take either one of those two avenues. One is to proceed through hearings through the Canadian Transport Commission; the other one under Section 64 is to proceed by order in council. This is the law. The law has a purpose. The purpose is that when something concerns more than a single line it is proper for the government to use Section 64. I will repeat that it is not the intention of government at this time to go the massive way, the way we did under Section 64 last July.

Madam Speaker, since it is the minister's intention not to go the route of unilateral action, and where possible to review it before committee and have hearings, would he at least give some credibility to that statement by agreeing not to terminate the VIA Rail service slated for September 6 from Havelock to Peterborough to Toronto, until he has at least fairly assessed the situation

July 12, 1982
Oral Questions
before proper hearings and has allowed those hearings to take place, in support of the Senate committee decision and recommendation that that process be followed, or will the minister continue on with unilateral action on September 6?

Madam Speaker, I do not intend to give such an assurance. In the statement issued last July we said specifically that the three routes in the Toronto area were essentially commuter routes. The Government of Ontario has taken over responsibility for the Barrie and Stouffville routes. The Havelock route, which goes through Peterborough, has been the subject of a mixed approach. Some of it will become part of the metropolitan commuter service, the other part will disappear because there is not enough traffic of an inter-city nature to justify its existence. But the Government of Ontario, I am quite sure, will very responsibly make sure that travellers in the area are served by other modes of transportation, for example, buses.

subsubtopic: OBSERVANCE OF SUNDAYS AND HOLIDAYS-PROVINCIAL RIGHT TO LEGISLATE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Justice. In March 1976, the Law Reform Commission of Canada submitted a report on the Lord's Day Act, in which it concluded that the federal government should repeal this legislation and transfer responsibility for legislating on the observance of the Lord's Day and other holidays to the provinces. I would like to ask the Minister of Justice whether, after the summer recess, he intends to table a bill to repeal the Lord's Day Act and transfer the right to legislate in this area to the provinces and the territories?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: OBSERVANCE OF SUNDAYS AND HOLIDAYS-PROVINCIAL RIGHT TO LEGISLATE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we received a recommendation from the Law Reform Commission a few years ago, and we are discussing the matter with the provinces, because we cannot repeal the legislation until the provinces have formally decided to pass their own legislation. Our discussions with the provinces are continuing, and if they wish to take over this jurisdiction, we are willing to withdraw from this area.

subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF CONTROL GUIDELINES TO CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister who indicated last week that
the government was sending instructions to federal agencies to hold the line within the general framework of 6 per cent and 5 per cent on any increases they approve. Did the Prime Minister include Canada Mortgage and Housing in the list of agencies which received those instructions, and does he condone CMHC, over the last two weeks, increasing the prices of homes it has available for sale in many parts of Canada by $2,000, $3,000, and sometimes more than $4,000 per unit, in spite of the fact we are trying to put downward pressure on the inflationary spiral?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF CONTROL GUIDELINES TO CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there are two questions, the first on the government's directive. 1 did indeed write to all ministers and instruct them to the effect that regulatory bodies under their jurisdiction should be urged to stay at the 6 per cent and 5 per cent limits, with the exceptions which were indicated by the minister in the House.
In the particular case of Canada Mortgage and Housing, I would have to take the question as notice in order to deal with it. However, this is obviously a case where we are dealing with the cost of money to CMHC, which is just as high for that corporation as for anyone else. If it is attempting to-the hon. member looks puzzled. CMHC has to obtain its money from the government or the private sector, and that will bear on the price at which it can resell houses in its possession. The hon. member may be rightly puzzled; I would have to take notice of his question and see if I misunderstood it, and obtain an answer for it.

Madam Speaker, while the Prime Minister is looking into the matter he might consider whether it does not seem rather ridiculous to raise the price on a home, which could not be sold at the lower price, in an effort to move it in the marketplace? Does he feel it is reasonable to increase the price, first, by approximately the amount of the government grant for the purchase of homes, new or old; second, to do this on homes which have been on the market for six or eight months in some cases, at a time when we are trying to put downward pressure on inflation, not upward pressure as CMHC is doing?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: The hon. member asks me if it seems reasonable. The way he puts the question, Madam Speaker, it does not seem reasonable to hope-
That is what I thought.
-that a house which will not be bought at a certain price will suddenly be bought at a higher price. But this is a theoretical question as far as I am concerned.
No, it is real.

Well, if the hon. member assures me it is real, I will look into the matter. It is perhaps something we should
July 12, 1982

review. But the hon. member will understand that unless 1 get notice of the questions, 1 cannot possibly know everything which is done by everyone, everywhere, all the time, on everything.
Some of the time!

subsubtopic: DEFENCE SPENDING REPROFILING
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Defence. The budget papers contain a reference to expenditure savings resulting in part from "defence spending reprofiling". Would the minister tell the House what exactly is meant by that phrase, and particularly the curious word "reprofiling"?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: DEFENCE SPENDING REPROFILING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the definition of "reprofiling" is, I suggest, using your judgment to see how you can save $100 million each year on the defence budget.
I know the second question of the hon. member is probably going to be how are we going to save $100 million on the defence budget, and I will answer it right away. I think this will be done through savings between the projected increase in remuneration paid to the forces, and the actual amount paid. I would like to mention too that the pay increase given last April to the forces remains in effect until next April. However, the projection was around 13 per cent, and we gave about 11 per cent, which means a saving of about $20 million for each percentage point.
Next year we have projected something like 10 per cent or 11 per cent, and according to the policy of the government, which we intend to abide by, we will give 6 per cent. We will save 5 per cent or 6 per cent, and this saving does not affect procurements or result in the cutting of personnel. It does not affect anything in the defence budget itself; it is strictly a saving.

Madam Speaker, the minister knows full well that the budget referred to military pay savings and defence spending reprofiling, and he has spoken only about the pay savings. He also knows full well that there will be no cuts in pay for the forces this year, yet the budget papers call for a $100 million reduction in the defence budget. Has the minister pointed out to our NATO allies that we are not going to be able even to come close to the 3 per cent increase in defence spending that we promised them and, for the fourth time in five years, Canada will not be living up to its promises?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 do not think the allegation of the hon. member for Victoria is exact. I think the 3 per cent has always been taken by all our NATO allies as an objective, on the condition that economic conditions prevail so that we can reach it. You have a good example in West Germany which is probably going to have a negative increase in defence spending this year because it cannot afford it. However, 1 can assure the hon. member that for the last seven years, as I have mentioned before, we have averaged about a 2.7 per cent or 2.8 per cent increase in the defence budget, which I think is a good performance on the part of this government.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), the minister in charge of destroying rail commuter service to the City of Barrie, stated in answer to a question by my colleague, the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm), that the province of Ontario was terminating the Barrie to Toronto train. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPLY OF MR. PEPIN DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: That is obviously not a point of order. Statements by ministers or by hon. members may be corrected only by themselves, not by other hon. members.

Madam Speaker, my point of order involves another example of the sloppy, sneaky, arrogant way in which the Liberal government governs our country. Today I received a notice advising that Bill C-201, an act to amend the Holidays Act, would be before the House during private members' hour on Friday last, July 9. The notice said that second reading would be resumed, but the notice has not yet been posted on the members' bulletin board. I found that this bill received second reading, went through Committee of the Whole and received third reading on Friday last, all in a matter of five minutes without a quorum in the House.
You were not here! You would not know!

I take exception to that. This is an improper way in which to pass legislation. I question the propriety and the legality of a law passed by fewer than 12 members out of 282. It is a sneaky, arrogant way of governing the country.

Madam Speaker, on this point of order, I would just like to say that as for the debate lasting only five minutes, we can assume that this is because the members of this House realized it was high time we took action. When hon. members are really determined, they can show the Canadian people that this House is able to proceed expeditiously with the passage of a bill that has been under discussion for some time, especially since no objections were raised by the Progressive Conservative members who were in the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: As far as I know, all the proceedings which took place Friday afternoon were entirely in line with the procedure of the House of Commons, and unless the hon. member can show me that mistakes were actually made and that there was a breach of parliamentary procedure, I do not think the House will want to reconsider the action it took Friday afternoon.

Madam Speaker, I suggest that hon. members should be notified in ample time when these bills are to be debated so that they can prepare to be here. This is simply another attempt to take everything that is biblical, and everything that is Anglo-Saxon, out of the laws of this country.

Oh, oh!
[ Translation]

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on the last point of order, first of all, it is true, unfortunately, that I was not aware of what happened Friday, although I was very happy to hear the excellent news that our colleagues who were present in the House had the
July 12, 1982

very good judgment to realize that the time had come, that Canada was sufficiently mature to want to call the first of July Canada Day.
Regarding the comment by the hon. member that members did not receive advance notice of the bill presented by the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), I can say that this is absolutely false. The hon. member must know that the list of bills to be debated during private members' hour is distributed in advance, and that Thursday, the day before, notice had been given to the representatives of his party, the whip and the deputy leader in the House, and the same applies to the New Democratic Party as is customary. In fact, we had hoped the bill would be passed during one of our very late nights but, unfortunately, the members present at the time were not yet mature enough; now, a few days later, it seems a miracle has happened and we have results at last. Therefore, Madam Speaker, there was not trickery involved. Hon. members received proper notice, parliamentary procedure was strictly followed, as you yourself indicated, and I think we should all be happy that from now on, we can celebrate the first of July as Canada Day.

Madam Speaker, I would like to point out two things concerning the business that came before the House during private members' hour last Friday afternoon. I did not see any bars on the doors to keep hon. members out.
Hear, hear!

I do not think anyone was prevented from coming in here. Hear, hear!

speechtext: Filibuster!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
The opposition House leader says filibuster. I suspect I had just fallen asleep for a few moments. I had intended to participate, but anticipated it would be much later in the day.
The other day I spoke on the budget noting, as I am sure most people have, that the budget was directed primarily to the problem of inflation. I suggested, and I repeat very briefly, that noted economists such as Thurow and others have always pointed out that in the case of inflationary trends there are winners and losers. These winners and losers achieve that status more often than not by misfortune rather than by good management. Winners are very obvious among Canadians fortunate enough to have savings in the banks and earning remarkably high interest. They are considered as winners. A company that can indiscriminately pass on its high interest rates as a cost of doing business to an element of captive consumers does not suffer abnormally from inflation. People whose salaries are totally indexed do not bear a fair burden of inflation. Nor do Canadians who for one reason or another

July 12, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
find their income to be relatively insulated from the effects of inflation.
The losers are much more evident. They include many business people who for one reason or another have to borrow at rates considered usurious two years ago in order to meet the payroll and provide a cash flow to stave off a recession in their plant for whatever reason. Also, the farm community must borrow money to buy seed. The fishermen must borrow either to repair or buy new nets. Then there is the home owner who innocently and in good faith bought a home one, two or three years ago and is now faced with the problem of mortgage renewal.
There are no winners and losers in unemployment. Everybody loses in periods of high unemployment. That is what is happening in this country. We now have close to a million and a half people out of work, people who for the most part would prefer to work. They cannot quite understand why in the space of 24 months a healthy, wealthy country finds itself with the type of economic problems we have before us.
As I mentioned last week, there are some areas in which nothing can be done by the Canadian government. We cannot control the price of commodities. We cannot restore the price of $1.20 per pound for copper rather than the present world price of 60 cents. We cannot do anything about the price of lumber, lead, zinc, gold or silver. Those prices will be increased and improved as the general economy of our trading partners improves. Our problem is that when their recovery begins, we must be in a competitive position to take advantage of their resurgence.
I do not think anyone considers an inflation rate of 12 per cent to be very competitive compared with that of the Americans, our largest trading partner. Therefore, it is imperative that all of us look at the problem of inflation to see what we can do both as a collective society and as individual Canadians.
Having suggested in the budget the other evening that there are winners and losers, we have tried to do something about the plight of the losers by deindexing our income, providing more money for the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) to allocate and distribute. He was able to indicate an increase in housing starts, giving financial help to that industry, which is one of our traditional ways to recover in this country. He was able to indicate some interest relief from high mortgage rates for people facing mortgage renewals as well as those who want to buy a home.
The minister was able to allocate funds to the business community, the farm community and the fishermen. He was able to do that because he asked other Canadians more fortunate, those who have an income that can be taxed, to share the burden with these less fortunate people. He asked us to do that by paying increased taxes and reducing to some extent our total protection against inflation through indexing in order to provide moneys to the government to help these people in such a way that we do not increase the deficit, which is of concern to some people.
Thurow and other economists quite often remind us that inflation has been an issue, a phenomenon if you like, which goes back thousands of years. In pure economic terms, the solution is fairly simple. Thurow pointed out four or five ways that inflation can be controlled. He quite properly points out that each and everyone of them requires a political decision. As one man's income is increased, another man's income must be reduced. The problem that all of us face is whose incomes are to be curtailed and whose are to be protected? How do we help the less fortunate? The budget has gone a long way toward doing that.
Thurow points out that not too many years ago Germany and Switzerland were able to curtail dramatically expansion money in those countries. This drove their unemployment levels very high, brought their inflation rates down and protected their currencies. They exported their unemployed back to their countries of origin, which were Portugal, Spain and others. He pointed out that the tight monetary policy in vogue now in industrial nations will in time produce the effect of reducing inflation, but he also pointed out that because of the time factor there will be damage, harm, stigmatization and unemployment. Those are the byproducts of this policy of absurdly tight money. When combined with the selfish attitude of the Americans with their high interest rates, which bear little or no relationship to their level of inflation, the problem is compounded for Canadians in all walks of life.
Thurow pointed out, quite logically, that voluntary controls are as effective and fair a way of controlling inflation as anything else devised. He also pointed out that this is not a perfect society and that everybody is in favour of restraint, provided they do not have to practise it.
In its budget this government has asked Canadians to restrain their demands and expectations voluntarily. Parliamentarians from all parties have answered that challenge, and that is reflected in the bill we are discussing, Bill C-124. Members of Parliament and members of the Senate have voluntarily agreed to reduce their pay increases to 6 per cent and 5 per cent over the next two years, recognizing that if this spirit of voluntary restraint can be extended across the nation to other public servants and other groups in society, this can go a long way to bringing inflation down.
No one has suggested, least of all the Minister of Finance or the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston), that the movement toward this voluntary restraint is something that is being accepted without question. However, it is encouraging to note that Thursday and Friday leaders of the business community and leaders of the labour movement gave some support- in fact, more than just a little support-to the concept. There is growing evidence on hot lines and radio programs and from the feedback we are getting that yes, Canadians are prepared to put a little water into their wine, as French-speaking Canadians are apt to put it, to restrain their demands and to accept less than full compensation for inflation in their pay increases, if they can be convinced that that money will be
July 12, 1982

used to help the less fortunate, to stimulate the economy, to get the housing market back on track and to recreate jobs rather than add to unemployment.
One point raised by some labour leaders-and with justification-is that they want some evidence that they will not be the only group making a sacrifice. They want some evidence that, if they curtail their demands, the business community will curtail prices. It is significant that as inflation drops 3 per cent or 4 per cent over the next year, there will be less and less rationale or reason for regulated industries and services to plead before regulatory bodies for increases in their rates to offset inflation.
The concept of sharing and voluntary restraint is something I think Canadians can live with. They are in fact a little intrigued with it and are prepared to adopt and support it. Nobody should attempt to tell the Canadian public that this is much more than rough justice, that there will not be some imperfections in the concept and that there will not be some people who will have to bear a different burden-unintentionally-from others. However, let us weigh the alternative. A million and a half Canadians are out of work, many for the first time. Many people have never known the need to restrain. Many have never lived in a period of recession or depression. What we are starting here could very well bring an end to growing unemployment and stimulate the economy. Slowly but surely it could create more jobs over the next six months and reduce unemployment.
I think people will respond. The challenge of the front benches is to make that message clear and with some passion and conviction. It is very, very hard to ask Canadians to join in a crusade against inflation if for some reason they think we are not fully behind it ourselves or if we do not think it can work. It can work.
In one of his later books, "Five Economic Challenges", Thurow drew the analogy between voluntary restraint and attending a football or baseball game. In the excitement of the game or a play people in the first ten rows inevitably stand, blocking the view of the people behind them. The people behind say, "If only they would restrain themselves, we could all see." In many ways this situation is the same. If we all restrain our demands over the next year or two, inflation will come down and we will all be in the same relative position. It will be painless but effective.
Are Canadians prepared to take this step? 1 think so. The alternatives are price and wage controls at some time-always difficult in a federal system-and more unemployment, until finally inflation drops with a thud and we start all over again the laborious, time-consuming and difficult job of restimulating the economy, reducing unemployment and putting people back to work.
I do not intend to get into the specifics of Bill C-124. I am not sure to what extent the President of the Treasury Board will want to amend certain provisions of the bill in committee. It seems to me that rather than deny collective bargaining in its entirety he might want to look at the arbitration route for
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
settling not only grievances but also other provisions in collective agreements dealing with safety, health and other conditions, which in many collective agreements are more important than money.
I suppose the one thing that motivated me to participate in this debate was that I have been somewhat appalled and concerned about some of the things I have been reading and hearing, both in the House and on radio and on television, which reflect total ignorance of the competence, sensitivity and humanity of our public servants. Perhaps I grew up in an era when no one challenged the fact that the Canadian public service was the best in the world. I still have that view because I have dealt with the Canadian public service for the last 20 years both as a minister and as a backbencher. Perhaps it is because I am a former minister of labour that I know the components of the public service. Public servants are not all Ph.Ds earning $75,000. They include the messenger and the cleaner-we used to cal! her the charlady-the jitney driver, the printer in the printing plant, the clerk and the stenographer. These are people we take for granted. They are fellow Canadians. They are decent people, but their earnings come closer to $10,000 than to $20,000 or $30,000.
It is unfortunate that somehow we think we have to stigmatize our public servants. I hear from people who should know better, in my own party and in the House, people who fail to understand that if you treat the public service as an equal, which it is, if you put your problems to them in a fair way, if you say that Canadians are not doing their jobs and remind them of it, you will find that they will respond in a very positive way.
When I first joined the Department of Labour, Mr. Speaker, it was a pretty rundown, demoralized department that was given to me. I found within weeks that the senior officials in that department could be stimulated, could respond if challenged and were prepared to participate in decision-making and in policy-making. I found to my surprise that 40 or 50 of them at least held a Ph. D. in economics, particularly in the research field. More than once I tried to probe as to why they had remained silent and why they were not participants. Sooner or later it came out that they tried in the past but found that nobody really cared, so why should they, they said.
We are bringing forward a bill to limit the salary increases of our employees, for very good reasons-because our employees are the people of Canada. There are employees, too, in the House, and the people of Canada, the taxpayers, pay them salaries as public servants, in increasing numbers. There are well over a million persons at the moment who have no income from jobs, so it is only logical and normal that those employees who have job security in the public service should restrain their demands and accept the provisions of Bill C-124.
I would hope that, in rationalizing the provisions of Bill C-124, the reasons for it, somehow we do not give the impression that we should reduce the salaries of public servants because generally they are overpaid and underworked and making a mess of it. Nothing is further from the truth. If you go into the

July 12, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
unemployment insurance office at the moment or into the Department of Manpower or into any of the places where people are dealt with, you will find tired, weary, polite, efficient people, whose workload increases as our population grows and as we demand more and more. I would be very upset if, somehow, at the end of all this exercise, we were left with the mistaken impression that somehow our public service is second to that of any other country in the world.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would plead with workers across the country to realize that voluntary restraint can be justified if for no other reason than that it works. Hundreds of thousands of unfortunate Canadians, fellow workers, want to get back to work sooner rather than later.
I mentioned this to a friend on the weekend who promptly referred to some labour leaders in a rather derogatory form. It is vital that the politicians should understand that there is a great similarity between Members of Parliament and union leaders. Union leaders must get elected too. They have to say some things sometimes in a rather harsh way. They have to generalize in their statements. They have to satisfy the majority of their members. They are elected by employed people, not by unemployed people. So when they appear selfish sometimes in their statements, they are speaking for their constituents, who are the employed, not the unemployed. That does not mean that they must not take into consideration the problems of the less fortunate. Probably many thousands of those who are out of work now would not have been so if this government had not been forced into a very tight monetary position. When people say there must be a better way, the better way is that we as Canadians agree to restrain our demands a little and bear some of the burden of the less fortunate.
Like everyone else, Mr. Speaker, I want to see some visible evidence of co-operation on the part of the business community. We want to see that this is not a one-way exercise but that they fully intend to restrain prices, that they fully intend to get behind the concept. Fortunately, their balance sheets or their profit and loss statements taken in the first three months indicate that the business community are very anxious and will have to be anxious about their falling profits and will cooperate with government and labour.
I would recommend, Mr. Speaker, that Bill C-124 be adopted as quickly as possible, so that it can go to committee stage. The minister may want to look at some of the clauses that appear to make the bill a little more difficult than it has to be. He may want to explore the possibility of referring certain matters during the life of a collective agreement to arbitration rather than freeze them entirely.

However, although the parties bargain jointly it would be wrong to think that the collective agreements are identical. In fact, it came as a surprise one year when I was negotiating a settlement in the railways to find that the CNR collective agreement was different in the west than in the east.
It was due to tradition, to particular problems, to problems of geography and the Fraser canyon, and many other things. As a general rule, as the hon. member said, the bargaining sessions are collective. In hard agreements such as of wages particularly, and things of that nature, they are always identical. In fact, the railways have always insisted that one group should be the same as the other rather than be different. This is a very valid issue to be raised at the appropriate moment with the minister in the hope that it can be resolved. The hon. member will appreciate, I am sure, as a former postmaster, that the same thing occurs in the post office. We try to have the same wages and the same basic conditions.
The whole point is that this bill cannot be expected to be introduced-and I said this earlier-at such short notice, as it had to be, and be totally equitable across the board. It cannot be. There will be winners and there will be losers. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to speak on Bill C-124 today. I agree with the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey) that it would be wise to get the bill into committee as soon as we can. There are some specific amendments which should be helpful to those affected and which indeed may be instructive to those who may be affected down the road.
July 12, 1982

At this stage, however, on second reading we are dealing with the principles behind the bill. I will not take the time of the House today to deal with some of the specifics that we will be dealing with in committee. I want to spend my time, Mr. Speaker, looking at what 1 think are the significant principles involved and some of the problems that arise from those principles.
I think the principles are three in number. Obviously, the first principle of the bill involves the question of restraint; second, the bill involves the principle of collective bargaining; third, the bill involves the principle of equity and fairness. I wish to deal with these three principles as expeditiously as I can. It might be helpful to spend more time on the principle of restraint than hon. members opposite have.
These days, restraint is in the air. Just the other day the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) indicated that he thinks restraint is so important that he is calling for a national crusade for the government's restraint program. The new banner line of the government has become sharing and cooperation. We hear those words daily from ministers of the Crown. All of those things are considered to be important in what the government and many people in the country regard as the problem of what to do about restraint.
Restraint is not a word or a concept that we have spent much time considering in the past 35 years. There is one simple, sole reason for dwelling on the question of restraint in the past year or two and perhaps for the next few years. Obviously we are concerned about restraint because of inflation.
Inflation is the problem of the eighties in the same sense that the depression was the problem of the thirties. There are some people who, for whatever reason, paid little enough attention to it. Inflation is the one economic category that steals from everyone, that destroys our ability to protect our future; it is the one economic category that hurts poor people and middle-income people far more than it does rich people. It is absolutely essential, if Canadians are asked by the government to join some national crusade, that they understand what causes inflation and that they see whether the proper remedies for it are being proposed.
Inflation is not new, we have had it for centuries. It was caused by wars, by bad harvests, by the infusion of gold and silver into the marketplace, by waste and mismanagement of governments and enterprises. We have always had inflation and the classic pattern was always the same. In good times, economic boom times, production went up, employment went up and prices went up. In bad times, in times of economic recession, prices went down, production went down and employment went down. What was new in the latter part of the seventies and the early part of the eighties was that employment is down, production is down and prices are up. That is the essential dilemma. Economists have no clear answer for dealing with it.
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
In this part of the twentieth century we have arrived at a time when we can no longer make clear sense of our economic situation. Employment is down, production is down and prices are up, so we have met the essential economic dilemma of our time. Moreover, inflation of that order is worldwide. Indeed, inflation throughout the western world and in many other parts of the world has become chronic, endemic, escalating and uncontrollable.
If it has become all of those things, then why do we not understand it better? If it hurts us so much and it has become so difficult to deal with and to root out and cure, why do we not understand it better? I am no economist but I know that, if we look back over the past 35 years since World War II, we see some changes which have taken place which would lead us to see what steps could be taken to curb inflation.
There are a number of reasons for inflation, Mr. Speaker. The first, and I think the most important, is our attitude to growth after the war. We felt that we should always have growth and that everyone should enjoy growth. The idea of growth became important. Everyone wanted it and for the first time in our history government assumed responsibility for it.
In 1949 the Government of Canada took responsibility for the level of employment in this country. Up to that time it had been left to the normal changes of the business cycle.
Why did this change take place? It was in part because of the depression in the thirties and in part because of the war. People wanted good times, not bad times. They wanted never-ending growth. During the latter part of the depression, during World War II and the late forties, we felt that through the economic theories of Lord Keynes we could control the business cycle and get rid of the chronic economic problem of boom and bust. As well, we were interested in never-ending growth because of the cold war. There was competition between economic systems. The result was that our attitude toward growth and our demand that the government deliver it was such that as the size and importance of government increased, its share of public spending and of the gross national product escalated.
By the mid-fifties we had established the essential link that the government was responsible for growth. At the same time we began to see the emergence of inflation as a chronic problem. That is the first reason for inflation, the attitude toward growth and the demand that the government deliver it at all times to all people.
The second reason is less clear but is perhaps more important in the long run. In the last 35 years we saw a new climate of expectation created. We established the idea of more, that everyone should have more. Everyone's family, friends and neighbours should have more. The idea of more began to be the significant attitude, the predominant attitude of most people. It began to replace some older virtues. We began to drop them off during the fifties, sixties and seventies. Hard work, thrift and frugality began to be submerged by the need for more, to the extent that even if we could not pay for more we sought ways to borrow in order to get more. That was true

Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
not only for people but for institutions as well-banks, for example.
I remember going into a bank when I was a lad. It was a very formidable institution with a high oak table and a little cage. Behind that cage and looking very severe was the teller. I was taking the money earned on my paper route to put it in the bank. I was taught that if I put it in the bank and saved it, I would learn the magic of 5 per cent. I would learn that if I worked hard and saved my money, I would get money in return. I knew that if I put it into that bank they would do the same thing, invest it. I went back to that bank about 20 years later, in the early sixties, and I noticed that all the oak tables had gone. The very severe teller had gone and the cage had gone. It was all very colourful. They had colour on the walls, people were happy and cheerful; but what really caught my eye was that there was a boat right in the middle of the bank floor. The bank was running a raffle, and the bank said that if I bought a ticket for $1 I could win the boat. I could get something for nothing. All I had to do was get the right number. I did not have to work for it, I did not have to guess, I just had to buy the right ticket. Our institutions and our people, Mr. Speaker, over 35 years slowly changed the traditional economic attitude that we had and moved into the concept of "more".
The third reason for inflation, Mr. Speaker, is that we began to feel we could control the imponderables of economics. We could control the business cycle. The war and the post-war period taught us that. We were unable to accept the proposition that bad times might come, that busts for businesses might come. We decided that was not acceptable and that we could control the business cycle.
Fourth, businesses learned that it was essential to control prices and stabilize markets; competition was not a good thing and was to be avoided by whatever method within the law. In short, the government began to provide a net not only for people but for business enterprise as well, and slowly the concentration of economic power by large corporations and large unions began to make a mockery out of the fact that you could manipulate prices by the simple mechanism of the market.
The fifth reason for inflation, Mr. Speaker, was that in order to have the other four grow, governments had to expand liquidity. They had to create money. The grease for "more" was money. So they began to expand the money supply.
All of those factors established the reality of inflation. It is worthwhile mentioning them again so it is clear, because I find very few of these addressed in the bill before us. Maybe there is more coming, but very few of these causes of inflation are reflected in this bill. First is the attitude towards growth and government responsibility for it, and therefore government's growth. Second is the philosophy of "more". Third is the assumption we can control the business cycle to suit our purposes. Fourth is the concentration of power, by both
business and labour. Fifth is the constant increase in the money supply to keep the rest going.
That, I think, is the shortest way 1 can point out what has happened, and the result of it all, I repeat, has been that inflation in the early 1980s has become chronic, endemic, accelerating and uncontrollable. Anyone not willing to face that fact is neither serving themselves nor indeed the people they represent.
We began in the late seventies and now in the early eighties, Mr. Speaker, to look at policies which might fix it up. These were policies which were used in various countries, more in some than in others, and different in some places than in others. Squeezing the money supply was used in a number of countries. There was cutting back on government spending, and raising taxes to limit consumption. Wage or price controls were imposed, or guidelines given. Economic co-operation was sought through an incomes policy. We lived, if I can describe it this way, and are living now in a world of stop and go. We have stop policies and go policies. The stop policies are to bring inflation down, but what they do is increase inequities and frustrations in people. When those inequities and frustrations get too high, we quit the stop policies and put in the go policies which allow us to deal a little more with the inequities and frustrations; but they, of course, cause inflation to go back up to where it was before. So we have gone around and around on the merry-go-round. That is our basic dilemma, Mr. Speaker, which we have not yet been able to deal with.
So the government has announced it is going to have a program of restraint, a national crusade. In order for it to work, Mr. Speaker, the government, like anyone else, has to answer the ancient economic problem posed in these two questions: Who gets to work? Who gets how much? Those are the fundamentals of economics.
As for who gets to work, in a period of growth we do not have to worry too much about it because new entrants and those displaced by technological change can get jobs. So the question of who gets to work is answered by growth.
As for who gets how much, when the pie is increasing and everyone's slice is increasing, that question is not a big problem. But when we have slow growth or no growth, when we have restraint, then we have to figure out what will be just and fair in terms of who gets how much. A program of restraint, therefore, requires the inclusion of two principles: one, that we have freedom of choice; two, that it be fair and equitable. A program of restraint which does not offer freedom of choice and fairness and equity will not succeed.
That brings me to the second principle, Mr. Speaker. This bill not only deals with the principle of restraint, it deals with collective bargaining. Since 1872 collective bargaining has been the way in which we in this country have solved the economic problem of who gets how much. This is not a happy time for the principle of collective bargaining because people have found it an easy scapegoat, aided somewhat by the abuse of the right to strike and confrontation tactics between labour and management.
July 12, 1982

Interestingly enough, however, most of the great successes in collective bargaining go unreported and unheralded. Year after year tens of thousands of collective agreements are signed and they become the way in which we decide who gets how much. In a free society it is the mechanism of collective bargaining which we have used to determine that question. I hope we never underestimate the value of the principle of collective bargaining. It struck me that those who have never been great supporters of that principle fail to understand that at the root of the whole question of Poland some months ago- let Poland be Poland-was the desire on the part of Solidarity to have the collective bargaining rights and privileges which Canadians have enjoyed for decades.
1 want to know why the government wants to throw out the principle of collective bargaining or why it wants to freeze collective bargaining. I am not talking about the right to strike here; I am talking about the way in which collective bargaining was used traditionally in the country so that people were able to see it as fair and equitable. For example, the government is saying that it wants to restrain compensation by 6 per cent in the first year and by 5 per cent in the second year. At the same time it is saying that that restraint will be applied to everyone, whether one happens to be a corporate president or a charperson, whether one happens to be earning $9,000, $10,000 or $109,000. It assumes rather sloppily that the progressive income tax system will take care of the inequities. It will not, and the government knows it.
Why does the government not add up the total amount which the 6 per cent and 5 per cent restraints give and then let the collective bargaining system distribute it, rather than impose it? The government will not obtain co-operation by imposing it. It could have exactly the same effect but allow the collective bargaining system to work so that it can be distributed fairly to people.
The collective bargaining system has allowed for stability in our industries. Anyone can obtain stability without freedom, anyone can obtain freedom without stability, but it takes years of learning, co-operation and tradition to create a system which allows both stability and freedom to exist side by side. For example, the country has benefited immensely for the past 90 years in the railway industry beause there has been the growth of the tradition of collective bargaining. In the railway industry there are 16 unions, 11 railroads, and 90,000 people. We have industrywide bargaining in the railway business, so there is one joint agreement.
I have here a number of agreements current over the next two years. They involve Canadian Pacific Railway, Canadian National Railways, Dominion Atlantic, Ontario Northland, Quebec Central, Algoma Central, Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo Railway, Esquimalt and Nanaimo, Toronto Terminals, Grand River Railway Company, Northern Rail, Shawinigan Falls and VIA Rail. Those agreements are with non-operating unions. I have another agreement involving the Shop Crafts and Locomotive Engineers. All railway agreements work

toward a joint agreement. That fact developed by railways and unions has given us stability over these many years. We should not underestimate this because the country is built on the railroads. We need for normal commerce, both internal and external, a transportation system which provides stability at prices we can afford. It has been worked out over the years by management and by labour. Indeed, there have only been three strikes in this century in the railway business.
Unless this bill is changed, it will bring to an end industrywide bargaining in the railway industry because it requires that CN operate under the 6 per cent and 5 per cent wage restraints, while CP and all other railroads do not. It not only affects the wages of employees, but it affects their benefits, their health and welfare schemes and their pensions. We will have people working side by side in the same job in the same shop and on the same locomotive for years at different prices and with different benefits, because different unions will be negotiating with different railroads for different workers at different times. They will never get it back.
When the bill goes to committee it is absolutely essential for the government to listen to what railway unions, management and the railroads have to say. Collective bargaining is a principle that is not only a nice one, it gives freedom and stability. At the same time it gives the economic stability we require for the normal operation of the commerce of the country.
My friend has just given me a telegram which is testimony to the points I have made with respect to the railroads. It is from the Vancouver Board of Trade and concerns the situation faced by railroads. It reads:
We fear that, if inequities develop in compensation paid by the two railways, there could be critical rail service disruptions. We ask your assurance that legislation will provide safeguards against this serious threat.
We must bear in mind that we are talking about unions which are the most responsible in the country. Unless there is a change in the bill, we are heading for short-term instability and long-term chaos in the transportation industry. The bill not only affects railroads, including CNR affiliates and wholly-owned subsidiaries, but the trucking industry as well.
The hon. member for Lincoln said that the bill was rushed through in a difficult time. This may well be, but it does nothing for people's confidence in the government because it is putting through a bill which will destroy 90 years of collective bargaining in the most significant industry in the country. It angers people that the government is not competent enough to think this through. When it comes to committee stage of the bill, I hope government members will go beyond their normal "Yes, we agree with cabinet", and think clearly about what witnesses on behalf of the railway unions, management and the railroads have to say.
Aside from the principle of restraint and the principle of collective bargaining, this bill touches upon the principle of equity. The government will not restrain anyone unless the person thinks it is fair and other people are being dealt with in the same manner. This is why people worry as they look at

how the government conducts itself with respect to other people.
It is not fair that the government can deindex income tax and cap wages, which make it harder for low-income people. It is not fair that the corporate president, as I mentioned earlier, is treated the same way in terms of the 6 per cent and 5 per cent as the charlady. It is not fair that those who receive perks of office-and we know who they are and what they are-such as hidden income, are not treated the same way as other people who are affected by the 6 per cent and 5 per cent caps. It is not fair that the government can put 6 per cent and 5 per cent restraints on the salaries of some people and we do not even know what are the salaries of presidents of corporations. Surely equity requires that the government put its cards on the table and tell us what these people earn; they are being paid by the public. It is not fair that the 6 per cent and 5 per cent cappings do not include fees of consulting and professional services directly for the government.

Lawyers in the Justice Department had increases of 11 per cent. It is these actions
which question the government's moral authority to implement this restraint program.
I might say that I agree wholeheartedly with the comments of my friend, the hon. member for Lincoln, that civil servants are easy to categorize and shunt around. But one can have nothing but respect for the people you work with who are working for the Canadian government on behalf of the people of Canada.
This brings me to the question of equity in terms of the public service. There is one figure which has always impressed me. Women fill only 4.3 per cent of senior management positions but comprise 82 per cent of the lower paid administrative and clerical positions.

They will be hard pressed to understand that any affirmative action programs within the public service that will be of any benefit to them will no longer be operated through the collective bargaining system, since it has been frozen by the government through this bill. Are we to think that this will contribute to the sense of fair play that the government's program is supposed to provide?
My colleague, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) talked about the national crusade and the crusaders. As we look at the national crusade of restraint we have to look at the tainted wings of the crusaders, because in the final analysis many people do not understand all of the program and the numbers, its applications and effects. For example, very few people understand that this is a bill not only dealing with restraint but one which takes away collective bargaining as well. People do not understand the consequences of the entire bill. That is why they very often do not judge by what is being said but by who is saying it; not by what is promised but by who is promising it. That is why, when it comes to the ability of the government to put through a wage restraint program in the public service, its chance of success is directly related to whether or not people regard what the government has to say as honest and believable. In short, whether or not they have any confidence in the government to carry out wage restraints.
That confidence has been undermined by government policy and government statements. For example, the fact that the deficit in the budget went up to $19.6 billion is not the most important factor. It is the fact that eight months ago the government said its deficit would be $10.5 billion. It is very difficult to have confidence in a government which makes a mistake in its understanding of the future of the economy in saying that its deficit would be $10.5 billion and it ends up at $19.6 billion. It is not only the fact that the deficit has doubled; the government could not see or did not know this would happen. It is bad enough that it doubled, but it is worse that the government did not foresee it.
The government showed its lack of leadership when it came in with a budget on November 12 which called for restraint and put its own spending at 22 per cent. It came in with its next budget on June 28, which again called for restraint and, indeed, wage restraint for the public service, when its own
July 12, 1982

spending for 1982-83 was increased by 20 per cent. People take their lead not from what is said but from what is done. This government has shown that it may be one thing for it to preach restraint but that it does entirely the opposite.
I conclude by saying that this bill is more than meets the eye. It is far less than meets expectations. It is not purely and simply a bill to restrict the wages of public servants to 6 per cent and 5 per cent. What is at stake is whether or not the government itself will be able to change in order to muster its own moral authority, which the country needs in order to have a restraint program. There is nothing wrong with restraint. There is nothing wrong with people recognizing again that the only way to progress is to exercise some frugality, and that the only way to make use of the country's natural resources is not by squandering them but by husbanding them.
While some people believe that we must exercise growth and optimism or else the belief will be that we will head in the other direction, most people in running their lives realize that if they do not look after their own resources and husband them, and if they do not discipline themselves, they will not be able to depend in the future on the bounty coming forward.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has said that he is challenging Canadians. I have never heard such arrogance in my life-that we need the Prime Minister to say that his job is to challenge Canadians into restraint. Anyone who walks along the street and goes into stores, factories or shops knows that for the last two or three years people have slowly begun to change. Canadians have said, "Sure, I want more, but I know that in order to have more I must remember some of the older virtues of working hard, thrift and saving.'' They also know that much is dependent upon themselves in their communities. That is why this bill, and this Prime Minister, I might say, are not on the cutting edge of change. That is insipient arrogance which words fail me to describe.
All the government is doing is desperately trying to catch up to Canadians, who understood long ago that if there is to be any salvation for this country it depends on them and their ability to change their habits and be able to make the country work. As they watch this government they know for sure that they cannot depend on it to do either of those two things.
