Mr. Speaker, before I begin my remarks I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) on an excellent analysis of the problems of world inflation. However, I think he failed to add two very important points to the five points he mentioned. What he did not say was that the world has been practising the lunacy of spending $500 billion of its income each year on armaments. If that kind of money is to be spent on armaments, it will not be used to feed, clothe and shelter hungry people or to provide them with warmth, sustenance and medicine.
I consider the other point he did not mention to be a very important factor. If it has not already made itself felt, it will affect our children in the future. For years, perhaps for even a century of industrialized society, we have been passing the social cost off to future generations. Future generations will pay for the frivolity with which we have treated our environment. We have used our air as a sewer and we will pay the cost in acid rain. We have used our rivers as sewers and we are paying the cost right now. This year, the Fraser River in British Columbia had to be closed to fishing, and there are probably many similar examples which could be cited.
We are concerned over the number of people who have been and will be deprived of jobs in Canada and perhaps throughout the world. We have not begun to have a glimpse of the impact of the technological society, the automated society, and what it will do to us in a relatively short time.
Bill C-124, derived from the budget, has all the earmarks of some attitudinal survey, as if it were based on something that pollsters like Martin Goldfarb or Allan Gregg might have come out with. Those pollsters have probably gone out and discovered that certain buzz words are accepted in society, buzz words such as "sharing", "co-operation" and "solidarity". These words are supposedly reassuring to the masses. They seem to pop out of every Liberal speech as if they were there because they had a particularly confident, caring sound. I could not prove it but I certainly suspect that

July 12, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
that is how it happened. The surprising word is "solidarity". The expression "solidarity forever", formerly had a mildly leftwing taint to it, but not any more, not since Lech Walesa. It is now perfectly acceptable and even polite in society; it has found a new respectability.
I think that if someone were to suggest that this budget was sort of whomped up, he would probably find that he was wrong and that this is part of a policy which probably goes back two or three years. Some would say that it is a conspiracy. I would not be so extravagant as to use such excessive language, but I believe it goes back at least two or three years. Its purpose was to soften us up for this day, when we are told "Tighten your belts and lessen your demands. We are threatened. Lower your expectations." The only thing the government has not said is "Tote that barge and lift that bale".
That is the sense of what we are being asked. The people of Canada are being asked to participate in a crusade. Guess who wants to lead us in a crusade to the promised land to slay whatever is slain in the promised land, such as dragons or infidels? The very infidels who got us into this trouble now want to lead us out of it, and they ask us to have confidence. The dragons are at the helm.
On the other hand, I hear an accusation from the Liberal side concerning anyone who has the audacity to complain that we do not want to become part of the 6 per cent world, the wonderful world of 6 per cent. I think all of us would accept that world if we felt is was a 6 per cent world of prices and profits, not just a 6 per cent world of wages. If we say that it will not work, as it did not work the last time, or that it is unfair or inequitable, we are almost accused by some of being disloyal Canadians because we will not fall for Bill C-124. I, for one, will not be accused of being a disloyal Canadian because I happen to analyse the bill and its intention somewhat differently from that of the government, the desperately cornered government which has made a mess out of everything.
We are told by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) that we cannot get ahead of our trading partners. What does he mean by that? Our trading partners in what? What do we sell, besides auto parts, with a high wage component? Wheat? That is 3 per cent of the economy. Lumber and pulp is perhaps 16 per cent. Does that have a high wage component? Ore is 11 per cent. The rest of it can be forgotten; that is, most of it. Who are these trading partners? They are the United States to whom we sell 73 per cent, Japan to whom we sell 6 per cent, and Britain to whom we sell 3 per cent. I do not understand how it can be said that our wages might get ahead of those of our trading partners, because what do we sell with a high wage component, to justify the stand that the government is taking? The only exception is auto parts and we are behind the United States in comparative wages.
People have a right to make judgments about the government, and they do make judgments about the government. I know that Your Honour's attitude will be that of an objective speaker. What would Your Honour think of a government that
allowed wages to fall behind inflation for five years in a row and then blamed the workers for inflation? There has been no wage-push inflation in Canada, but we are certainly paying for it with the loss of 1,200 jobs a day. A small community of jobs is going down the drain each and every day. In the last six months 100,000 manufacturing jobs have been lost in Quebec alone.
Let us compare our wages with those of our trading partners. In 1980, manufacturing wages were about $11.94 per hour in West Germany. In the U.S. they were $9.92 per hour; in Canada they were $9.06; in Japan they were $5.88; in Britain, they were $7.07. What were the increases in the period since 1975? Wages in West Germany have gone up 91 per cent; in the U.S. 56 per cent; in Canada 48 per cent; in Japan 95 per cent; and in Britain 116 per cent. Canada has fallen behind for five years in a row. We have the lowest wage increase since 1975, but we are told that we have wage-push inflation. We are told that we must somehow lessen our demands, we must do with less and have less security. More of us must be out of work and more of us must pay high interest rates.
What is the situation in Japan? That is a major competitor for manufactured goods. The Japanese have a lifetime job promise not to be fired at the whim of a company such as B.C. Tel or Bell Canada. They receive bonuses every six months if a company earns a profit. Whoever heard of bonuses here? All one sees is confrontation. Japanese who work for corporations receive low-interest loans when buying homes, and the use of vacation cottages if they need a summer holiday, as probably most of us do. There is much government-industry planning. Those are the privileges in Japan compared to the type of security of the average Canadian or, for that matter, American worker. It is no wonder that the Japanese are willing to cooperate.
Supposing we do all of this and supposing we accept the 6 per cent solution, what will be the quid pro quol What will the government do for us? Will it guarantee, for instance, that we will have lower land prices or lower prices for anything that we purchase? Of course not. It will do exactly what it did the last time: it will freeze workers' wages at 7.5 per cent and let inflation go to 9 per cent. We did that in 1975. That is why some people are a little cynical about joining this crusade. It is a little hard for us sometimes, just a little bit difficult. That is one example.
What would you think, Mr. Speaker, of a government which robs people of their homes and businesses through high interest rates and then brings in a budget which does nothing about that? We heard the musings of the minister of housing about lowering interest rates when he appeared over national television on the weekend. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was asked about that today, he either feigned or proved that he did not know anything about it. I do not know what people feel about their promises.

A lady in my constituency sold her house on May 28. She put in $25,000 and got out $1,900. She says at least they do not owe the credit union anything. That family took a bath. She is a school teacher and cannot afford that kind of expense.
1 listened to what high interest rates have done to one businessman. Tie has been in business for 25 years and has a $1,200,000 mill. He pays the bank $6,000 a month in interest. The bank shut him down. That put 56 people out of work. That is what high interest rates have done. We are asked to take less, to limit our demands to 6 per cent, no matter who it is. What is the government going to do about prices or interest rates? Silence, deafening silence.
In 1980 bank interest was 2.6 per cent above the inflation rate. Today it is 8 per cent above the inflation rate. We now hear that some banks are in trouble, that their profits are down. They certainly deserve to be down; they have almost had a Roman carnival for the last two years. If their profits are down slightly these days, I do not think anyone should worry too much about that. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) said a few months ago, the banks ought to bleed a little.
What would you think of a government that signs deals to increase petroleum prices 30 per cent per year, 10 per cent on July 1 alone? It is taking $1.8 billion more out of the hides of consumers. It wants us to limit our demands to 6 per cent, but refuses to try and negotiate energy deals. These 10 per cent, 10 per cent, 10 per cent increases every six months will mean that by 1986 the same people who are frozen to 6 per cent and 5 per cent will be paying $1,900 to heat the average home and $1,700 to drive a car. At the same time, world oil prices are tumbling, falling from $40 a barrel to $32.50. We are still pumping up our prices. Esso is in bad shape. It had to lay off a lot of people. A year ago its profits were $140 million; now they are only $40 million. Esso is really hurting. That is the third example I would give when asked to make comparisons and join a crusade.
What do you think of a government that is prepared to give away billions in order to push Candu reactors on every tinpot dictatorship in the world? This government was prepared to give the Mexicans two $6 billion Candu reactors, depending on the life of the contract, up to $1 billion each in export development or payment subsidies, interest subsidized loans. The government was going to borrow at 14 per cent and give it to the Mexicans at 7 per cent, simply for financing.
The school teacher in my constituency was paying 22 per cent interest on her home. Mr. Speaker, in the circumstances perhaps 1 may be forgiven for saying that it would occur to an objective observer that there is a certain lack of commitment evident in the feelings of some of those who have suggested that they see something unfair in the legislation before us. The manner in which they are jumping at the opportunity of expressing the grievances of those who will suffer as a result of Bill C-124 shows that their fervour is somewhat lacking. That is not surprising in view of some of the contradictory statements we have heard from members of the official opposition in the last while. I hope it is simply an aberration and that they will find their consciences and their feet in the next few hours and days.
In commencing my remarks on what I consider to be one of the most damnable and discriminatory pieces of class legislation that I have had the misfortune to consider since being elected to this chamber of horrors, I feel compelled to warn
July 12, 1982

you, Mr. Speaker, and any other possibly faint-hearted member that the deep feelings I hold on the nature of the subject before us may cause me to slip or, perhaps to put it more appropriately, to escalate into what might be described as lunchroom terminology, backwoods vocabulary or just plain speaking.
I shall try to restrain myself but these feelings are not mine alone; they are those of many people I have worked with over the years. They are so strong that it may be difficult to restrain some of the more volatile expressions and terminology that may be appropriate. I make no apology for that because, in spite of the fact that I have been a member of what is sometimes ludicrously called this House of Commons-and I have to wonder at the word "Commons" when we deal with legislation of this kind-for some two and a half years, I am still an industrial worker and a trade unionist in conscience and at heart. I am proud of that. I feel compelled, in spite of the sometimes phony sophistication of this place, to call a spade a bloody shovel.
As a prelude to the statements and accusations to come, I should also say that the Conservative Party will invoke my wrath and anger every bit as much as the Liberal government, because in spite of its mealy-mouthed and hypocritical effusions of mock protestation, Bill C-124 is a classic example of that party's thin blue line of knee-jerk reactionary conservatism in practice.
When it comes to the rights, needs and legitimate aspirations of honest, hard-working people, the shallow, hollow little men and women of the Conservative Party to my right are every bit as mean, deaf, dumb and blind in the political and economic sense as are the overstuffed apostles of Liberalism across the way.
Bill C-124, an act respecting compensation in the public sector of Canada, is bad law. It is unfair, it is unwise, it is discriminatory and it is counterproductive. It is based upon a lie and it is wrong. Quite simply, it is an attack upon the very spirit and soul of a democratic society. It seeks to place the burden for our society's ills on the shoulders of those who are the servants, not the masters, of Canada's governmental and economic system.
I should like to quote from a document that is rather well known in the annals of western democratic evolution, the Magna Carta of 1215. Part VI of that document reads as follows:
Clauses to control the behaviour of royal officials, particularly those of local government. No town or individual shall be forced to make bridges or maintain river banks-
Nothing could be more clearly designed to show the absolute moral bankruptcy of a government that chooses as a scapegoat for its own ineptitude and failures the servants of the people, the public employees of this nation. The Magna Carta was presented to King John in the year 1215. Because some of those opposed to him were referred to as those who robbed the rich to give to the poor, one can only assume that what he was representing, and what this government which is acting like him represents, are those who would steal from the poor to give to the rich. Relatively speaking, that is exactly what this bill is about.
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
We have heard a lot of talk about crusades. Perhaps we need some more crusaders but different from those of 1215. Perhaps we need someone who will attempt to seek some form of redress or an appeal for justice on behalf of those rendered powerless, either to help themselves, or to have any significant say in what to do or how to do it for the majority of their waking lives, namely, when they are at work.
The actions of the Liberal government and the Conservative opposition in this situation remind me of a parable related to me and the leader of this party, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), by an old Doukhobor gentleman who called in to us during an open line show in Trail, British Columbia, some two and a half years ago. He told us that the Russian people have a saying that, "no one ever mentions the wolf; it was the goat that ate the sheep." That may be very simple but it is surprising how close it is to the truth in the present situation. No one is talking about the wolf being to blame for the present situation but somebody sure is looking for a goat.
We are in a desperate situation in this country, Mr. Speaker, and we all recognize that. I gather from some of the things that were said at the meetings between the government and the provincial premiers, between representatives of the federal government and the business and corporate leaders and between leaders of the Canadian Labour Congress and the government in the last few days, that things may be more desperate than anyone has admitted up to this point. We would be among the first to agree that if times are as tough as they appear to be, it is going to require much more of a coming together and much more of a spirit of true compromise between the different interest groups in our society and representatives of political parties than has been normal over the past few years. If we are to achieve that in a constructive way, then there must be some acceptance of good faith on the part of all parties involved.
It is a hollow appeal to ask of working people in particular but also ask of those who have not had the opportunity for some months and years to engage in remunerative work to make the first sacrifices.
A young plywood plant worker from my home town of Nelson, B.C., wrote some words on the subject last November, about the time some 100,000 people gathered on Parliament Hill to protest the high, avaricious and usurious level of interest rates that were threatening to drive many people out of their homes. His words say a lot about attitudes justifiably held by many people at this point. I should like to take the opportunity to put on the record of the House the words to a song that this young man wrote. In clear and in more understandable terms than many of us are capable of expressing, they recount the horrors and feelings of anger and frustration of many people. Those are not phony words, Mr. Speaker. They were written by a young single parent who last week was not only told that he was going to continue to be laid off after having worked for not more than two or three weeks since last fall in the plywood plant in which he has some eight or nine years' seniority, but that the mill was closing permanently. That mill is one of only two major industrial operations in my home town and his. He is angry and his neighbours are angry.
If people think-not only some people in government but some people in some corporations-that they can use this opportunity to squeeze concessions on working conditions, safety and many other things won by hard struggle over the years, then I think the operative phrase is "every dog has his day". Any employer who has been in the industrial relations business knows that it does not pay to milk everyone for everything you can get because of a temporary advantage, because they will find a way to get even. They may have to hurt themselves in the process, but they will do that because they are very human.
The government thinks that by Bill C-124, Mr. Speaker, it can impose a law which will not only restrict incomes of public servants but will also eliminate for that period of time the
entire process of collective bargaining. I do not know what kind of mentality it is which makes the government think it has the right to take away fundamental human rights in this manner. Even if one was to concede that there is a right in desperate times to put a ceiling or a cap on wages, there is absolutely no excuse for them denying the very process of jointly attempting to determine the conditions of your work, whether you are going to live or die on the job, and all of those other matters so vital to the interests of ordinary people. By so doing, the government will sow and reap the whirlwind.
In trying to analyse the kind of mind which gives rise to this sort of action, one can only assume that there are many in the government who think, "Well, we gave them these rights so we can suspend them." The right to withdraw one's labour, Mr. Speaker, was not given to anyone by government. It was won on this continent when working men and women found that by exercising their right to withdraw their labour they could gain some appreciation and recognition of their problems and appropriate grievances-without laws setting out when and how they could do it. When that right was found to be effective, not only by working people themselves but by the rest of society, that is when governments across this land and in the republic to the south began to recognize that right in law. The right was not given, it was simply claimed and recognized, and in being recognized it was thereby limited and structured.
I am not debating here whether or not that was an appropriate action. In a civilized society we attempt to structure our conflicts in ways which allow for an appropriate peaceful method of decision-making among different sectors. Industrial relations and employer-employee conflicts have been stabilized in a better and healthier way for society at large than what we see in some countries in Europe, particularly eastern Europe, which have never adopted the necessary democratic structures to allow ordinary working people to freely determine their own destinies and the conditions under which they work and live. Instead, they have had the kinds of explosions such as we have seen in Poland simply because they have never come up with the kinds of structures necessary for people to sort out their problems in a democratic and reasonable way.
The spokesman for the Conservative Party who spoke prior to the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose) made some very constructive comments, Mr. Speaker. Madam Speaker, I feel constrained to enter into this debate because of the blatant inequities in Bill C-124. I would remind the government at the outset that the last time they brought in wage and price controls, the year following the lifting of those controls the government was defeated. I think that is something which the treasury benches should take into consideration at this time, if not publicly then certainly privately in caucus and cabinet discussions.
Of late, there have been many references to the fact that we are no longer in a recession but, rather, in a depression. In many respects, the recession or depression that we are in today is even worse than the great depression of the 1930s. The stockmarket crash took place in October, 1929, as we went into the winter of 1929-30, and the bottom had fallen out of everything by 1931. Wages had gone down to virtually nothing and there was massive unemployment. Prices fell to rock bottom as well. The vast majority of the people of this country, of the United States and of western Europe felt that they were all in the same boat. Oh, the very rich weathered it quite nicely in Capri, in Nice and in West Palm Beach, but they were such a small, insignificant group in the western world in terms of numbers that people seldom thought about them except when

they went to the nickel movie in the afternoon and saw how the very rich were living. Generally speaking, virtually the entire population felt the depression and suffered as a result. Consequently, across our country there developed a sort of esprit de corps. People said, "We are all badly affected by this great depression and we will have to pull together on our own." They said this because the damned government under R. B. Bennett was doing nothing, like this government here in Ottawa. So they decided to pull together by themselves.
1 can recall those days of hardship back in the 1930s. They were days of hardship, but also days of togetherness when families got together and shared. I can recall growing up in Sault Ste. Marie, which was one of the hardest hit areas in central Canada. If there was one empty seat in a car heading out to Lea's Bay or Pointe-aux-Pins on a Saturday or Sunday, one called up a neighbour and made sure that that seat was filled by a person who could not otherwise get away to the beach. My father was the head of a Gilbert and Sullivan operatic society and he was able to call dress rehearsals for 10 o'clock on a Monday morning because the non-professional cast had no work and there was all kinds of time to work together and to play together. In that depression, as severe as it was, with the soup kitchens and bread lines, there was a feeling of common suffering. Everyone was adversely affected and therefore everyone on the block, in the neighbourhood or the community was pulling together. There was no feeling of alienation toward some groups in society, although some were hurt more than others. There was no feeling that someone in Ottawa was trying to rip off something from them or that people in some parts of the city were better off than those in other parts.
Today, however, we are in a very pernicious kind of depression. We have widespread unemployment, with 1.3 million officially unemployed. There are probably 1.7 million or 1.8 million in total who are unemployed. Yet we still have 10 million people working in this country. Also, we have rising prices at a time of mass unemployment. There are also some professional or self-employed people who are making more money in 1982 than they made in 1981.

Today we are in a situation where those who are in dire straits are being told to tighten their belts, to deprive themselves even more, and we all face rising prices and costs. Now we have unemployment insurance and welfare, two things that we did not have in the 1930s. I can guarantee that without welfare and unemployment insurance, we would have soup kitchens and bread lines in many cities across Canada today; in fact, in most cities. Therefore, when we compare the depression of the 1930s with the depression of the 1980s, I believe those who are suffering today are suffering more than those who suffered in the 1930s because they know of the inequity which is being perpetrated and advanced by Bill C-124. It states that all federal public servants will receive an increase of 6 per cent this year, 5 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984. Therefore, those at the top will not suffer nearly as much. In fact, they will not suffer at all from the decrease in their income from 1982 to 1984. But those clerks and those who clean out our public buildings, those who do menial work in federal service, will have relatively bigger cutbacks or losses in revenue next year, and they will hurt even more. The bill is simply not fair.
Of course, the primary aim of Bill C-124 is not directed at the federal civil servants. It is directed at provincial and municipal civil servants and the entire private sector. However, the private sector employees have already been hurting. As an example, I could name but three companies in my own constituency, in my home town of Brantford, namely, White Farm, Massey-Ferguson and Trailmobile, which have been suffering from wage constraint for the past year and a half. Their employees work for regular wages for three or four months and then they drop down to unemployment insurance for another two or three months. Then they are back on regular wages when called back for three or four months, and then again they are back on unemployment insurance. As a matter of fact, it has been estimated that if a White Farm employee had worked a full 12 months in the past year, his income would have been roughly $21,000 or $22,000, but with all the lay-offs resulting in the collection of unemployment insurance benefits, his gross income has dropped to about $15,000 or $16,000. That is a wage constraint. Yet the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) says that it is greedy businessmen and greedy workers who are forcing the government to curtail the increase to our old age security recipients. How much nonsense does the Prime Minister think that this side of the House can continue to endure? We will certainly not accept it as an argument. As a matter of fact, it is the spuriousness of the government's arguments with respect to this recession or depression which causes us to refuse to accept virtually anything it now says on that side of the House.
The government goes from one public relations disaster to another. It does not have its financial and economic act together. I say that because in order to find a new solution or way out of this recession, the government has again resorted to a failed program which it attempted in the seventies, the AntiInflation Board of 1975.
Let us look at some of the figures at that time as far as the Anti-Inflation Board is concerned. In 1974-75 also, the government blamed wages for forcing up the cost of living and prices. We know that not to be true. At that time the New Democratic Party said it was not true. It was later proved not to be true, that we were right.
We are asking the same thing today. The government says that wages have to be lowered in order to bring down inflation. We have the data to support our argument that wages are not causing inflation in this country today. It is not a wage-push inflation. The government is resorting to this as a spurious argument, a cheap means of bringing in controls.
Let us look at the failure of the previous controls exercise of the seventies. Whan the Anti-Inflation Board was introduced in 1975, the rate of inflation was 10.6 per cent. The target of the AIB for bringing inflation down was 8 per cent in 1975, 6 per cent in 1977 and 4 per cent in 1978. Those were the targets. Instead, inflation was only slightly moderated. When controls were removed in 1978, lo and behold the rate of inflation was 9 per cent. It was down about 1 per cent after three years of wage controls and some price controls.
Price controls were not equitably enforced. I recall listening to some businessmen and professionals joking in 1976 and 1977 that their incomes were actually going up much more rapidly than the AIB was permitting because they were getting phony job promotions. That was the most common way of circumventing the wage controls at that time.
In 1975 the annual rate of unemployment was 6.9 per cent. During the control period, it moved steadily upward. Controls caused unemployment; 7.1 per cent in 1976, 8.1 per cent in 1977 and 8.4 per cent in 1978. One reason for this is very obvious. When you take money away from consumers through lower increases in pay, you are taking high velocity money out of the marketplace and are depressing demand. When you depress demand, you cut back on productivity. When you cut back on productivity, you increase unemployment. It is a vicious downward spiral. This stupid government cannot get this through its thick head. I do not know how much pressure we in the opposition and the people of Canada have to bring upon this government to make it see some common sense and understand some basic, fundamental economics.
Let us look at some wage settlements under the AntiInflation Board. According to a government paper, wage settlements during the AIB program were brought down from almost 20 per cent in 1975-it was actually 18.6 per cent in the second quarter of 1975-to 7 per cent in 1978. According to a Conference Board study on the AIB program, controls resulted in the loss of several thousand jobs, a drop of 8 per

I have just given the facts. We have a model to go by, the Anti-Inflation Board from 1975 to 1978.

Mr. Speaker, before we took recess for dinner, I was trying to impress upon the government that its approach to fighting inflation by trying to control public sector wages was the wrong approach. I tried to point out to the government that the major causes of inflation today are basically threefold. The first reason is the very high interest rates or the real interest rates that are running around 8 per cent or 9 per cent above what they should be. That is a major cause and accounts for slightly in excess of two percentage points of the consumer price index. The second is energy taxes, on everything from home heating fuel, natural gas, diesel fuel and gasoline, a 30 per cent increase last year, another built-in increase of 27 per cent in 1982-1983. Again, this accounts for about three percentage points of the consumer price index. And, of course, the third reason is the cost of imports. In fact, imports are becoming so costly that Canadians cannot afford to buy a lot of the imports and that is why we have a favourable balance of trade with the United States-it is not because we are selling them more but because we are importing less. The reason we are importing less is that we have less money and we simply cannot afford it.
In those three areas alone we have at least six percentage points of the consumer price index. If it is running at about 11.5 per cent, it would have us down to about 5.5 per cent of real inflation. It would be as low as the average annual inflation rate in the United States. Instead of this the government once again is looking for a scapegoat. It is very typical of our Prime Minister to blame someone else. The Prime Minister says: "I never made a mistake in government." The Prime Minister never would admit to making a mistake. So, as we did in the year 1975 with the Anti-Inflation Board, again now in 1982 the government says: "It is labour, organized or unorganized."
But this time they cannot get a consensus right across the country. The provincial premiers will not agree, so he cannot invoke that section of the old British North America Act that allowed him to impose wage and price controls in 1975. Instead of that, he is attacking the federal public servants, hoping it will spin off into the provincial civil services and then to civil or municipal services and to the private sector.
When we come to the private sector, Mr. Speaker, we realize that honestly, even there the wages have not been inflationary. As late as 1980, Canada was seventh in hourly compensation, that is, wages and benefits in manufacturing, in

Life insurance to the amount of $10,000 will be provided for each salaried employee, the opportunity to purchase attractive group rates additional insurance at totals of one time to two
times less the basic $10,000, the annual salary, will be afforded each employee, and so on. That is based on reduced salaries.
That represents a 19 per cent cut in pay. It need not be legislated. The market forces presumably forced this upon the company, which in turn forced it upon the employees. This is the kind of mess that the government has got the business community into.
Specifically, Mr. Speaker, with respect to Bill C-124, the most pernicious and most contentious aspects of it are not really the compensation aspects. What is going to happen if this bill is passed without any changes in committee? For one thing, there will be no collective bargaining for two years on any issues-not just on money matters or income but on any issues. There will be no negotiations on technological change, on job categorization, on work loads, on overtime, on maternity leave, on any affirmative action groups.
We know, Mr. Speaker, that those who will be most adversely affected by this lack of ability to negotiate will be those at the bottom, the women in the federal work force. They are those with the lowest paid jobs, the most menial work, the least skilled. Once again, they are those who will have to take it on the chin. The professionals at $50,000 and $60,000 a year, I am quite sure, are not going to suffer all that much. But those earning under $20,000 or $25,000 a year will certainly be hurt a great deal.
Another matter which really angers me has been raised in the question period. I was absolutely outraged when I read in the newspaper that on the very day the budget came down 473 lawyers in the federal Department of Justice received a 10 per cent increase in pay. They received that increase just a matter of hours before the budget was introduced. As I said in my speech, earlier this afternoon, this government is going from one public relations disaster to another. It is as if hon. members opposite have no experience in government. And to make matters even worse, the inequities in this bill simply bring out their warped approach to the economic problems facing the nation today.
How could hon. members opposite possibly allow 473 lawyers a 10 per cent increase in pay just a few hours before the budget was introduced and then turn around and expect civil servants, who have already settled their contracts, to have their salaries knocked back to a 6 per cent increase when their contracts terminate? This is reprehensible behaviour by the government and cannot be allowed to go unnoticed and unchallenged.
The average Canadian is prepared to accept his or her responsibility in fighting inflation and in trying to get the economy moving again, but the average Canadian is not prepared to allow this government to be deceitful and dishonest in its approach, first, to the causes of inflation and, second to the cure. In the first place, we have a perfect example of a government refusing to admit that it should share a great deal of the responsibility for causing our inflation instead of blaming every other country in the world for it. Second, I
July 12, 1982

challenge the government to accept that the major causes of inflation today are high interest rates, energy taxes and the high cost of imports, and to come clean with the workers of Canada and say: "We appreciate it is not mainly your fault and that there are other causes, but we are asking you to do your share to get the economy going again." If hon. members opposite took that approach, they would probably get a more sympathetic reaction across the country. However, by bringing in Bill C-124 and legislating wage controls, the government is blaming the men and women workers of this country for the mess we are in today.
The most depressing problem of all is what to do when controls come off. Everyone, naturally, will want to scramble to catch up; the economy will get going full steam again and overheat. If we are to have wage and price controls-and I am not saying we should-for heaven's sake, let us bring them in at a time when the economy is overheating. The economy is not over heating right now. It is dying. It is almost stone cold. We have 31 per cent underutilization in our plant and manufacturing sectors. Is that the time to constrict further the money supply in the country? Hardly. This is the time to increase demand and increase spending so that we can increase productivity and get more people back to work. That is the argument I have used throughout the budget debate, and 1 use it again in this debate on Bill C-124.
My time is almost up. 1 am very dissatisfied with the intent of this bill. I am fed up with the all-encompassing aspect of the bill. I am fed up with the deceit of the government, the spurious economic arguments of the government and the reason the government gives for bringing in wage controls. The government is still dodging the major fundamental economic problems facing Canada and individual Canadians.
Until we get the real interest rate down to about 2 per cent, which is 2 per cent above the inflation rate, we will not stimulate the economy. We will not stimulate investment. People will not be prepared to expand their businesses or open new ones. Until we get some control over skyrocketing energy costs, we will have very high inflation, and as long as we have to rely on imports with a 77-cent or 78-cent dollar, again we will have inflation.
The government has addressed the wrong reason for inflation. It refuses to accept any degree of culpability for causing inflation, and it is not really attacking the main causes of it. Instead, it is making scapegoats of workers once again.
When I began my speech before the supper break, I said that the government is wrong in its approach. Just one year after AIB wage controls were removed the government was defeated, and I can very easily predict this evening that one year after these controls are removed, in 1984, the government will be defeated again.
In conclusion, I will paraphrase Shakespeare by saying the following: when is the winter of our discontent ever going to be made glorious summer by a change in government?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak, and I will be fairly brief. I hope I will not take quite as long on this important topic as the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) did.
I want to divide my presentation this evening into three parts. Hon. members might like to call the first part a rebuttal of some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Brant. The second part will be a description of the differences in political philosophy between hon. members on this side of the House and hon. members opposite with respect to the problems presently afflicting the nation and the problems which have caused hon. members opposite to bring in Bill C-124. Third, I would like to deal with some of the specifics of Bill C-124.
Before saying one or two unkind things about the presentation made by the hon. member for Brant-of course, not about him personally-I would like to compliment him on his presentation tonight. 1 think it was one of the best speeches that hon. member has ever made, at least from a technical point of view. I have difficulties with some of his reasoning, but he did make some good points.
I think the hon. member summed up the socialist approach to problems when he said quite explicitly that it was deplorable that some self-employed entrepreneurs had made more money in 1982 than they had in 1981. How terrible it had been-

speechtext:
This just illustrates the socialist ideology that everyone should be reduced to the same level of mediocrity and to the same level of misery.
1 take quite the opposite point of view. Any businessman or entrepreneur who made more money in the difficult times of 1982 than in 1981 deserves to be congratulated. In my opinion people like that have accomplished something. Anyone who has managed to do this must be possessed of a disproportionate amount of good luck or, if not that, a superior ability. Such a person must have worked harder and with more diligence than the very many people who, because of conditions beyond their control, lost money during that period and did not make as much as they did in previous times.
What are the benefits derived from people who, because of the extra effort they expended, were able to do better for themselves and, consequently, for the nation? Who pays the taxes in this country? It is not the people who are out of work and it is not the businesses on the verge of failure; it is the successful people who work hard for what they have. They pay the taxes that enable us to give subventions to the people not as

July 12, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
fortunate. Who is hiring workers in the country today? It is not the businesses on the verge of failure; it is the successful ones that are providing the few jobs that there are. They are paying better wages than those on the verge of bankruptcy. They pay better wages to get the people they want, and that is good. Who are the people making investments so that Canada will be strong in years to come? It is not the people who are losing money but the people who are making money. If the hon. member for Brant had his way, presumably the few remaining successful people would be taxed out of business. They would do what many other Canadians have already done, vote with their feet! They would be forced to leave the country, taking their money and investments with them. If that were the case, everyone would lose.
What we need to do in this time of economic hardship is to give all the encouragement possible to those people who are proving that in difficult times they can still make a go of things. We should not be telling them that they are not wanted in Canada because they are doing a little better than anyone else. Instead, we should be encouraging them and making it as easy as possible for them to do better. That would benefit the government and the citizens of Canada.
This afternoon I listened intently to the speech of the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey), a distinguished member of the House for many years. But I took exception to some of the ideas he presented. He seemed to be saying that what we are engaged in is a zero sum game; that in order for any one group of people to benefit, those benefits have to be extracted from another group. It reminds me of a poker game where people play for so long, and after an allotted time the winnings of some will balance the losses of others. I do not agree with that idea at all. We should be promoting the increase in the general wealth of the country. We are not engaged in a poker game. We should be engaged in the development of the resources and the people of this country.
The hon. member for Lincoln stated that controls are necessary. That is a favourite idea of hon. members opposite and of hon. members to my left. When it comes to controls and the influence that the state should have in the lives of people, their ideas are not very different; they both want controls.
This afternoon members of the NDP pretended to be against Bill C-124. I guess they have to say that because they think they have a lot of political support from organized labour, although I am not so sure; organized labour thinks for itself and does not do everything the NDP tells it to.
I listened carefully to what members of the NDP had to say. They were not saying that they were against controls. They were saying "Controls would be fine if we had wage controls here and price controls there. We just love those controls. Give us all the controls you are capable of." That is the way they really think. The NDP would just love to be welcomed back to the bosom of Beryl Plumptre. I can see that in their eyes, Mr. Speaker.
Let us consider what effect this zero sum approach and consequent controls have had over the lifetime of Liberal governments for 30-odd years. They are the reason we are in the state that we are in today. This is not something brought about by two or three months of action or inaction; it has developed in this country as it has in many others, as a result of policies pursued for decades.
Social services are a good example of my point, Mr. Speaker. Everyone in this House wants to ensure that people who are not so well off as some others get a break. I do not think that anyone in the House would be against that idea, although we have different approaches on how to accomplish it. Very little good has come from the leftist policies over a 30-year period with respect to increasing the incomes of people who receive the lesser proportion of income in the country. In 30 years there has been no significant difference in the proportion of income those in the lower 10 or 15 per cent of the population receive. The figures provided by the Welfare Council of Canada and similar organizations show that the only appreciable difference is that 30 years ago a larger proportion of the income of the lower 10 or 15 per cent of the population came from wage employment. Today, the biggest proportion of their income comes from government transfer payments. The wage component has been reduced.
In making this rather minor change we have built up a huge administration to handle the various transfer payments. We have accomplished a transfer from productive Canadians not to the poorer sector of the economy but to the administrative class, that is, government. The administrative class has a vested interest in controls. There is nothing that would make them want to change the system.
1 believe in the principle of expanding wealth, Mr. Speaker. If we are to generate the expanding wealth of the nation we do not need more controls put on society by the state, but less controls. There must be more freedom for individual initiative. That is the direction we must take, Mr. Speaker. There must be a reverse policy to that which has occurred in Canada and in many other countries over the last 30 years.
One of the differences between the depression of the thirties and the Liberal depression of the eighties must be kept in mind if we are to devise solutions to the problems facing us today. In the thirties, the depression was associated with chronic deflation. The prices of farm products, manufactured goods and labour were continually going down. In those days, with that type of problem, it is quite possible that it might have responded to the policy of deficit spending, printing more money to prime the pump. I have my doubts as to whether that really worked in the later 1930s, but at least it made sense to make the attempt because it might have resulted in beneficial effects. However, what has happened is that after times got good again the government, instead of taking more by way of taxes to build up reserves so that when times became bad again, when the business cycle had turned full circle, it could pump those funds back into the economy-which 1 understand
July 12, 1982

was John Keynes' hypothesis-the government said, "Look, we have run up these deficits, we have printed money during bad times and we should continue to do it through good times to make those good times even better." That is what we have been doing for decades. It is like a drug addiction, you keep having to have more and more of the drug of deficit spending and consequent inflation in order to get the same kick. We have gone about as far as we can go now, and in the Liberal depression of the 1980s we cannot use that same technique anymore. We have such a high debt now and we are running such high deficits-a projected $20 billion this year and probably higher-that we cannot print more money to bail ourselves once more out of the problems that this government has got us into. We have to think of different solutions to that problem because the Liberal depression of the 1980s is one associated with chronic inflation, not the deflation of the 1930s.
As 1 have said before, in the 1930s it made sense for governments to try new initiatives to get the world out of that situation, but in the present situation I think that government is more of a hinderance than a help. The government is already too far involved in society, in particular the economic aspects. If we are to cure this problem, it is not by more deficit spending, more inflation and more controls, but by the very reverse.
I think only the private sector of the economy can get us out of the mess this government has got us into.
As to Bill C-124 itself, Mr. Speaker, I personally do not like it. I think the government, on which should fall the responsibility for this economic situation, is asking Parliament to bail it out. Public service salaries are not really a matter for legislation. Parliament should not be asked to dictate what salaries and terms and conditions of employment should be. That is a matter which rightfully belongs, in my opinion, to the executive branch of government. It is their baby, Mr. Speaker. But what has happened? The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston)-and I do not condemn the person presently holding that office because it has happened over many years- and his staff, his senior negotiators, have failed. They have allowed things to get ahead of them. They have not exercised the proper restraint in their collective bargaining. So what they are doing now is admitting failure. The government is saying, "Look, we cannot do the task that was rightfully ours." It is now coming to Parliament and saying, "We have entered into all these agreements, and we should not have because we cannot keep them. Please, Parliament, save us from ourselves by passing legislation to undo the wrongs we have done."
I think, Mr. Speaker, that Bill C-124 is a con job. All the policies that go with it, the so-called budget of June 28, are con jobs. It is a con job when you ask business and labour to co-operate in the fight against inflation and at the same time the government is running up a deficit of $20 billion, possibly more, which will guarantee that inflation will continue into the foreseeable future. The likely result of this type of policy is an even greater portion of the national income being transferred from labour and business to government. It is a con job which will result in even more interference by government and a

greater proportion of the gross national income being spent by government. This will lead to a worsening of the problems, it will not help to make them better.
I dislike the blanket approach of Bill C-124. I think proper management, a function of the executive branch not the legislative branch, requires flexibility. Each task which must be done has to be judged on its own merits. If this were done correctly, perhaps we would find there should be increases given in some places, and reductions in other places. The government should keep in mind the market forces as they affect the rest of society and perhaps use that knowledge to determine what public service salaries should be. But the blanket approach of 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent next year will not increase the effectiveness or fairness with which the Public Service of Canada is treated. I think one of the things we could do to increase the efficiency of the public service is to rid ourselves of many of the levels of command which have been built up in the last 15 years or so. It would be better if many of these levels were reduced and there was much closer association between, say, the deputy minister and the people in the public service who are actually providing the services. The bill has been gone into by many of my colleagues and members on the other side. They have come up with a number of very specific problems contained in the bill. The inequities between CN and CP employees, the question of indexed pensions for public servants when the premiums have already been paid and the question of non-wage negotiations, will undoubtedly be dealt with in committee.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that as far as I am concerned the whole package means one thing: the Liberal government has failed, and the public no longer has any confidence in this government. What we want, sir, is not wage or price controls, or any other control. What we need in this country is a Conservative government which appreciates the way the economy operates.

The difference of opinion and difference of intention are unique to this side of the House. While I am convinced that I have colleagues on the other side of the House who feel similarly split with respect to their views, I can assure Mr. Speaker that when the division bells ring there will not be a single member on the

Unfortunately that circumstance has weakened very substantially the principles upon which the House has been based. The absence of free expression of legitimately-held views by members of the House has led in many circumstances to a great deal of disrespect that the general public has for the way in which some of our functions are performed.
Let me simply say with respect to Bill C-124 that it is divided basically into two parts. There are three, but the two essential ones are those which deal with public service remuneration and those which deal with the remuneration of Members of Parliament, Senators and judges. If I may deal with the second part first, today we are faced, as Canadians responsible for the passage of legislation which will govern the affairs of our fellow Canadians, with a very serious responsibility. The country as a whole is suffering. There does not pass a single day while I am here or while I am at home that I am not confronted with genuinely expressed anguish from some of my constituents who are suffering from our economic troubles.
Last Friday before I left, I received a call from a constituent who until two weeks ago had been operating a business which employed 24 employees. There are now 12. Those 12 people have families, responsibilities and homes. They have built a future in my riding, as have 1,300,000 Canadians across the country, and now find themselves without genuine employment. For a period of about a year they are entitled to take what amounts in many cases to half remuneration in terms of a payment from the unemployment insurance fund, and after that has expired, they become recipients of welfare until that too expires.
This is no time for Members of the House to be insulated from the problems which exist in the country. For that reason, 1 find it incumbent upon me to show at least some personal restraint, and I accordingly applaud the government for having introduced a piece of legislation which bears down heavily on Members of Parliament and Senators, since we are the only group under this bill who will actually take a reduction in remuneration. It is appropriate because it is here, quite frankly, that the responsibility for the economic morass exists. Collectively we are responsible-on this side for permitting that side to ever form the government, and that side for creating the mess in which Canada finds itself. Accordingly we should not benefit from inflation which the government creates. After all, it is only with respect to a reduction in expectations for the future, subject, as I have said to the effect of an existing reduction in the actual salaries paid today to Members of Parliament and Senators. Others who are to benefit from the relative security of their positions because no job is secure-and now I wish to pass on to the first group affected by this legislation-in some way should be called upon in a fair and reasonable fashion to bear some of the burden. It is a small burden indeed that is imposed upon them. They are asked simply to take less of an increase-a 5 per cent or 6 per cent reduction in the increase which effectively would operate today, trying their known increases to 6 per cent and 5 per cent over ther next two years respectively.

I will not deal at this stage with the rather complex way in which the bill is drafted, setting out the year of commencement, the termination of the years and the way in which contracts currently in existence are to be protected until they terminate. I seriously doubt that if one were to ask the average public servant in Canada-and I am not talking about the senior bureaucrat-"Do you, Sir, feel it appropriate, having regard to the special circumstances of your employment, to the fact that your employer will never go bankrupt officially, and to the fact that your fellow citizens cannot even find jobs, that you be called upon to restrain your demand upon the economy?" When the government had an opportunity to take intelligent steps toward recovery the government and its backers refused to do it. Now, when the time has gone it looks upon the public service as an appropriate whipping boy for its own failures. However, it is significant that it has tried to do something. Personally 1 do not believe that what it is attempting to do will remedy the problems of inflation in Canada, but it may have a desired psychological effect.
The Prime Minister likes to talk about frightening the hell out of Canadians. I prefer to think that our severe economic difficulties have made Canadians, who are reasonable people, convinced that they each have a part to play in the regeneration of our economy.
I have indicated that I believe that the public service will respond positively. 1 also believe that this may have a beneficial psychological effect upon labour movement negotiations. We know that the UAW is about to enter into rather intricate and important negotiations with the automobile industry. We also know that our automobile industry in Canada is suffering. Without the co-operation of the general public, wage restraints and the $100 million to be saved next year and the $800 million the following year are but a drop in the proverbial bucket in which the government has sprung so many leaks.
Another cause of our dilemma has been government spending. Government spending currently exceeds $90 billion per year. Part of this has been brought about by the unfortunate economic situation in Canada. But we must ask ourselves how

The interest charges on the national debt alone exceed $17 billion as anticipated by the budget papers delivered on June 28. In this respect I am thinking of Canadair with liabilities of $1,400 million. Quite frankly, this company would not exist were it not for the government guarantees. The government has run wild with the public purse. It is endeavouring in this small, minuscule way to recover some of its credibility. The government is to blame for the circumstances which all Canadians are suffering from. It is to blame for the heritage of debt which will be carried by our children and grandchildren and for as long as anyone alive today will be able to forecast. That is the great bequest of the Liberal administration to future generations. That is robbery. It has pillaged the pockets of the children and the unborn of this nation. It has tied them down with burdens and provided nothing for the days of emergency such as we are in now. It has squandered the heritage which was left to us when we were young.
I support the bill. It is the only sensible piece of reasonable effort that I have seen from the present administration. It is regrettable, unfortunate and lamentable that this is all that the government has to offer. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) stood in his place on Friday and suggested that the public follow the lead of the government in its restraint program. them and who have worked for them, and I will use the assets to pledge against the debts of our ludicrously stupid administration". No one can follow the lead of this government on any road other than the road to insolvency.

J. McDonnell, the former auditor general of Canada, and Ken Dye, the present Auditor General. I wonder to which comment he referred. I am looking forward to the day when that government will have the courage to admit that our businesses have failed and our unemployment has increased, because we, having ruined the economy, and having recognized the close relationship between interest rates which must be paid in Canada and the value of the Canadian dollar, have employed high interest rates to keep Canadian dollars at home and preclude Canadians and others from selling them in exchange for more attractive U.S. currency. Will they now admit that it is a farce that is perpetrated every Thursday, much to the agony of Canadians, wherein 90-day treasury bills establish the rate fixed by the Bank of Canada, which is then, in some magic way, used as a signal to the chartered banks to increase interest rates? The chartered banks do not borrow from the Bank of Canada either on Thursday or at any other time. All this government has done has been to shift the responsibility for interest rates directly from the Minister of Finance to the Governor of the Bank of Canada. That responsibility is one that has crippled not only small but also large businesses in Canada. That interest rate burden cannot continue to be borne by either industry, business or home owners. It is certainly true that the value of the dollar would be greatly enhanced if the government could cut its expenditures and if it did not have to rely upon the artificial fixing of high interest rates to maintain its credibility. Who, indeed, would want to invest in Canada when the government has done its best to drive Canadian business out of the nation and when it has done its best to add tax burden upon tax burden? In the November budget there was an increase in taxation. In the June 28 budget, there was a further increase in taxation. Curiously enough, both increases were equivalent to $1.3 billion. The voracious appetite for additional taxes, added to the Canadian ownership charge, the hidden charge on petroleum purchases, the shifting of the excise tax to an ad valorem basis, the shifting once again of the manufacturers' sales tax to a wholesale tax to gain further and further revenues, were all designed to leave less and less in the hands of the
consumer and the production sector of the economy and to put more and more in the hands of the government.
But the government has not shown any inkling that it has learned its lesson, that it must indeed pare its own expenditures. We on this side of the House have begged the government to refer the estimates to a special committee of the House for examination and reduction. There is not an hon. member on the government benches who does not believe that somewhere in those estimates is a fund that is wasted. We all know that they exist. Who is better able to take an axe, to take a chainsaw and to cut through that dead wood and actually reduce the expenditures of this government than hon. members of the House of Commons?
We have urged the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport, when acting for the Prime Minister, to clearly show that the government's intentions are noble and that they will in fact do something positive to let the nation know that we are about to accomplish something, namely to accomplish the reduction of our own extravagance in this place. But it will not happen. They are too proud. They have never made a mistake in their lives. They are afraid to admit their errors.
There is not a Canadian who does not recognize that errors have been made. They look to those people on the government benches to stand up and say, "I insist upon cutting out the waste. I insist upon giving you good value for your money." Until that happens, the effort we go through here today with respect to this bill is a waste of time. However, as small as it is, as insignificant as it is in the total scheme of things, although it is deficient and inadequate, I feel compelled-since it is the first time and, having regard to the conduct of this government, it is probably the last time that I shall ever see anything worthwhile from it-to vote for it.

The hon. member for Western Arctic said that we need to give successful businesses the opportunity to do better. The fact is that the profits of Canadian corporations are down over 40 per cent this year over last year. The major corporations which were always the most successful have borrowed billions of dollars from the Canadian banks for the purpose of takeovers. They promised to pay the interest on those short-term loans. Many are now unable and are not paying that interest. Many of the largest mining corporations are now paying from 75 to 150 per cent of their total cash flow in interest payments on loans. They are hanging on by the skin of their teeth.
The hon. member for Western Arctic was critical about the $20 billion deficit. We all are. However, he did not ask the reason for the deficit. He did not ask why it had almost doubled in the last six months. If he were really interested and had looked into the matter, he would realize that the deepening recession has meant that unemployment has risen by almost 50 per cent.
There are now 1,300,000 unemployed who are no longer paying income tax. They cannot buy the goods they used to so they are not paying the sales tax. Because business is down, the corporations are not paying as much in taxes. Workers who

used to pay taxes are now collecting unemployment insurance benefits or are on welfare. That is why we have a deficit.
Both the hon. member for Western Arctic and the hon. member for York North criticized the deficit, saying that it had to be cut. However, they did not say how it should be decreased. We can see how the President of the United States could have got that country's deficit down if he were not increasing so substantially their military expenditures. He was getting down their deficit by cutting back on medicare, medicaid and hospital insurance, none of which are as good as the programs we have in Canada today. He also wants to cut back on social security. I wonder if the hon. member for Western Arctic wants us to cut back on old age pensions. The President is cutting back on assistance to universities. Those kinds of cuts would get our deficit down. If that is what the Conservatives want, they ought to say so.
I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Western Arctic compare, I thought favourably, the thirties with today. In the thirties there was no unemployment insurance, pensions, real welfare system, medical insurance or hospital insurance. The people suffered. Many starved. Now we have in place-not as much as we should have in my opinion-what President Reagan calls a safety net, the kinds of programs I have talked about. If I understood the hon. member for Western Arctic, and this is not a criticism but a statement of fact, he has a very high percentage of people in his constituency who are unemployed, who need assistance from the government such as unemployment insurance and welfare. I say that the hon. member for Western Arctic was not speaking in their interest when he made the kind of remarks he made this evening.
Let met turn now to the bill we are considering. What is the purpose of this bill? I read very carefully the speech last Friday by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston). If I understood correctly, he was arguing that inflation is caused by high wages and high wage increases which workers have been able to negotiate, and that it is these high wages and high wage increases which have led to the present inflation crisis that we suffer.
Wage increases in the past few years have been less than the increase in the cost of living. How can we blame Canadian workers for inflation when their standard of living, their take-home pay has been reduced in the last five years rather than increased?
We are told that in order to get inflation down, we have to limit wage increases. The government proposes that we start with federal public servants and that we restrict their wages increases for the next two years to 6 per cent the first year and 5 per cent the following year. The President of the Treasury Board compared unfavourably the wage increases which Canadian workers have been getting with wage increases in the United States. He pointed out that their rate of inflation is 6V2 per cent and wage increases there are about 7 per cent. With 6'/2 per cent inflation and 7 per cent wage increases, workers in the United States, at least those who are working, are able to maintain their present standard of living. What the government is proposing for our public servants is that, at a time

Let us keep in mind, Mr. Speaker, that bad as that is, despite the fact that the rate of inflation in the United States is down now substantially, a week ago interest rates in the United States were running at 17 per cent. We have been told that if we get the inflation down, interest rates will come down. That has not happened in the United States and it would not necessarily happen here.
Unemployment in the United States is running at about 10 per cent. Many of their basic industries-steel, auto, construction, housing-are dead or dying. We are told that if we bring wage increases down to 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent the next year, inflation will come down. In answer to a question last week the President of the Treasury Board suggested that if we did this, by this time next year inflation would be down to a
6	per cent rate. Mr. Speaker, that is not the experience we have had. I see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is here. If I give the facts which I am going to give about the AIB period incorrectly, I am sure the minister will take the opportunity to correct them.
At least in the 1975-1978 period, when we had the antiinflation experiment of that time with the AIB, we were supposedly to get wage and price control. Wage increases were to be restricted, but the rate of inflation was to come down from 10.5 per cent, which it was in 1975, to 8 per cent the next year, to 6 per cent the following year, and to 4 per cent the year after. Mr. Speaker, that did not happen, of course. Sure, wages were restricted, salaries were restricted, there were limits, but there were also exceptions. The minister knows about them. There were no real attempts to put a cap on selfemployed people. Doctors, lawyers, architects and engineers did very well, but wages and salaries were controlled. What happened to the cost of living? There was a decrease, a fairly marked decrease in the first year or year and a half. But by 1978, when the rate of inflation was supposed to come down to 6 per cent or 4 per cent, the rate of inflation was running at 9.5 per cent.
This time, Mr. Speaker, in this proposal, we are not even pretending that we are going to do anything about prices. This time we are going to depend on goodwill, on good-heartedness. The Minister of Transport shakes his head, indicating that I am not correct. I would love to see him get up after I have finished speaking, to show me where I am wrong.
There is no evidence that the private sector will voluntarily restrain itself on prices. Of course, at the moment prices are coming down because the sales are not there. We cannot give away some of our products. Copper prices, nickel prices, zinc prices, are right down to the lowest point to which they have been, some of them, in this century. We cannot sell these products, not because the wages are too high or because prices were too high a year ago or two years ago. We cannot sell, Mr. Speaker, because the traditional purchasers in the United States find that their economy is even worse than ours and they cannot buy the things we used to sell them. They are not producing, they are not selling cars, they are not building homes. Homes are not selling, so the lumber and the nickel and the iron ore and all the other products which we used to sell to the United States are not being sold.
We are told that the government has directed the regulatory agencies to keep their price increases down to 6 per cent. What kind of cynical nonsense is that? The Government of Canada made an agreement with the Government of Alberta and the then Government of Saskatchewan, so that the price of oil went up $2.25 a barrel last July 1. It will go up $4 a barrel on January 1, 1983, and will go up another $4 a barrel on July 1, 1983. That is an increase of over $10 a barrel. Every one-dollar increase in the price of a barrel of oil adds 0.5 per cent to the cost of living. So we are looking at an increase of 5 per cent in the costs of living by next summer, just because of the increase in the price of energy.
When the Prime Minister was asked by the Leader of the New Democratic Party to try to get the producing provinces to forgo all or part of the agreed-on price of a barrel of oil, he said, "We cannot do that, we have an agreement with the producing provinces." It is interesting that we cannot change an agreement with the producing provinces on the price of oil, but we can bring in special legislation, which we are discussing now, which will wipe out agreements signed in good faith, after a good deal of bargaining, and made under the laws of this country, between the public servants and the Government of Canada.
What does this increase in the price of energy mean? I ask the Minister of Trransport, if the price of diesel fuel goes up 30 per cent by next July, how in the world can the people of Canada believe that freight rates will not go up by more than 6 per cent? The railways will not be able to absorb that kind of increase in oil prices without increasing the prices they charge for moving freight. How will the airlines not pass on that increase of 30 per cent in fuel which they use on the aircraft to the airline passengers? It will be more than a 6 per cent increase in the cost of travel to people travelling by air, by bus, by rail or by automobile. It has to be, if the price of gasoline goes up by 30 per cent. Telephone rates are going up. Bell Canada has asked for a 20 per cent or 30 per cent increase, as has B.C. Tel. Hydro rates are going up in every province because hydro rates relate to the cost of oil.
What about some of the products the prices of which are set by regulatory boards? We control the price of eggs, we control the price of chickens, we control the price of turkeys, we control the price of butter. In the production of those things, the same increases must occur as also for almost everything else which the farmers produce. Energy makes up a very large percentage of the cost of produciton. If the price of energy goes up by 30 per cent, as it will under the agreement between the federal government and the producing provinces, the price of the food which is produced by Canadian farmers will have

to go up; and it will go up by substantially more than 6 per cent.
As other speakers have already said, over 1.3 million people are unemployed. As I pointed out a few moments ago, that is an increase of 50 per cent over the number of unemployed this time last year. Some of our major industries, the backbone of Ontario-manufacturing, our auto industry, our steel industry, the mines and the forest industries-have suffered major layoffs. Why? Is it because wages have been too high? That is nonsense. The lay-offs have taken place because the economies of the industrialized world and the economy of Canada are in a recession, and so we cannot sell our nickel, our copper, our zinc or our lumber. This is not because the wages of workers are too high. We cannot sell them because there is no market, and there is no market because of the recession created, to a large extent, by the high interest rate policy of the U.S. government, a policy which is followed by the Canadian government on the advice of the Governor of the Bank of Canada, who could have been fired. In fact, he did not have to be fired. I think his term of office was up when the Conservatives were in government. If the Conservative government had had the sense to follow a suggestion the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) has recently made-that is, that there should be a major turnover of senior public servants when a new government takes over- perhaps we would have had a different Governor of the Bank of Canada who would have recommended different policies.
