safer you are, which reminds me of the observation made many years ago by Lord Keynes that if one borrowed 100 pounds from a bank in Britain and could not pay it, that person was in trouble, but if a corporation borrowed one million pounds and could not pay it, the bank was in trouble. The bank could not let that corporation go down the drain. That is exactly what is happening in Canada.
If we want to get our rate of inflation down, as the government says we have to do, then the government has to do something about interest rates. However, there is nothing in this bill and there was nothing in the budget in June which gave any indication that we are likely to get our interest rates down.
Interest rates are likely to stay high or go even higher because when the U.S. government has to go to the market to borrow the $140 billion or $150 billion for the deficit it projected this year, it will drive interest rates up because there will not be enough investment money around to meet the requirements of both the American government and the private sector in the United States. When that happens, our interest rates will go up again.
What high interest rates have done and what they are still doing is to destroy any hope of industrial expansion. They have destroyed the construction industry. The housing industry in this country is dying. The purchase of farm machinery, automobiles and house appliances has dropped to a level we have not seen since the 1930s. Business bankruptcies are up by almost 40 per cent over last year. We are likely to see 10,000 business bankruptcies this year. Farm bankruptcies are up 60 per cent. What is alarming is not just that the number of bankruptcies of businesses and farms is up; what we are seeing is farms, which have been owned by the same families for the last 100 years, going bankrupt or selling out because they cannot meet the financial demands. What we are seeing is business, which grew and survived the great depression of the 1930s, going bankrupt in the recession of the 1980s. Our plants are working at less than 70 per cent capacity. It is pretty obvious to anybody who has any common sense and looks at things realistically that if we want to get our plants working to greater capacity and if we want to get more people back working in our plants, we should be increasing the purchasing power of the Canadian people so that they can buy the products which Canadian plants can produce.
Instead of doing that, what are we doing? The government proposes to reduce the purchasing power of Canadians by $2.6 billion. That is twenty-six hundred million dollars. How is the government going to do it? It is going to do it by capping the indexing of old age pensioners-those who already have so little-by deindexing income taxes and by capping and limiting the wage and salary increases of federal public servants to 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent in the following year. That will not bring down the rate of inflation. It will simply increase the number of unemployed in this country. Capping and limiting the wage increases of the 6 per cent of the labour

force in Canada which is employed by the federal government, by Crown corporations and by the armed services will not deal a body blow to inflation, so obviously the government is sending a signal to other jurisdictions. Obviously the government wants the private sector to follow suit. Obviously the government wants other public sectors to follow suit. In the private sector, where there are unions and where there is real collective bargaining, unions do not need to be told that they cannot demand from their companies more than their companies can afford to pay.
I wish the hon. member for York North would talk about labour negotiations with some knowledge and some understanding rather than with the prejudices he always brings to this kind of discussion. He implied that if workers are militant in their demands, if they go on strike occasionally and do not want to settle for less than the increase in the cost of living, this is the fault of their leaders. When he makes that kind of statement he shows how little he knows about the real world of workers and their unions. In recent years there has been case after case where union leaders have negotiated agreements, recommended them to their union, and the members have told them the agreements are not good enough. That happened twice in Sudbury. I am not saying that the workers were right or wrong; I am simply saying that they exercised their democratic rights. They were not led on or misinformed by their leaders. The hon. member for York North should find out more about the subject before he makes such statements.
Just as workers in the private sector will not voluntarily agree to a restriction on wage increases of less than they think industry can afford, neither will workers in the public sector employed in the provincial and municipal governments or the universities, schools and hospitals. The federal government would only see that restriction on wages and salaries if the provincial governments would pass legislation not only for their own employees but for those in the municipal and other publicly operated sectors of the community. Not many provinces will do that.
In my view this bill is a public relations operation, and a cynical one at that. The government knows that the public blames it for the economic disasters of high unemployment and high inflation. But the government has no programs to deal with inflation and unemployment. It knows it has to look as if it were doing something, however, so it proposed controls for the public sector.
Some people feel that public employees are all guaranteed lifetime employment, which is not true, and that they are all highly paid. They hear about deputy ministers who make $80,000 or $90,000 or $100,000 per year and about the Governor of the Bank of Canada who received an increase in salary to bring it up to $110,000 per year. They do not know about the tens of thousands of people who receive the same or less wages than they do, say $10,000 or $12,000 per year. The hon. member for York North assured us that if public servants were told why they had to make a sacrifice, they would be willing to do it. He certainly did not talk to any of the people like I did in the last week.
I am not concerned about whether the senior civil servants get a salary reduction or a freeze. Members of Parliament and senior civil servants are doing quite well. An increase of 6 per cent for senior public servants means that those making $80,000 to $90,000 or $100,000 per year will receive an increase of $5,000 or $6,000. In the budget of last November the Minister of Finance reduced the marginal tax rate for all big earners from over 60 per cent to 50 per cent, so they are already saving $5,000 or $6,000 as a result of that change.
At the time the senior civil servants had their income tax reduced, tens of thousands of public servants who earn from $11,000 to $20,000 per year will be restricted to a 6 per cent increase in the coming year. The President of the Treasury Board has predicted that the cost of living will increase by 6 per cent but it will probably go up by 9 or 10 per cent. Yet these people will be restricted to an increase of $500 or $600 in the year.
Last Saturday I took the time to meet some of the people who work for the federal government, Mr. Speaker. I will not suggest that I met a scientifically assorted sample that would give me a picture of everyone in the civil service. I was interested in the problems of the people who work for the federal government in the lower paid jobs, and I met half a dozen of them. Let me tell hon. members who have not met such people what it means to them.
1 met a woman who works as a cook in Winnipeg for the Department of National Defence. She is paid $10.43 per hour, $417 per week or $20,016 per year. She is married but her husband is unemployed. He had been taking a course which he has not finished yet. There are three children aged three, two and six months, and her husband looks after them while she works. She pays $450 per month for rent, so they cannot afford to go on holidays or go out for dinner. She told me they have not been out for dinner in the last four years.
Another woman is a cleaner also working for the Department of National Defence. She earns $8.06 per hour, $1,288 a month or $15,456 per year. Her husband works part-time for the City of Winnipeg in the works and operations department, but he has been able to get full-time work and is only employed for about five months of the year. They pay $172 per month for rent, $72 per month for heat, and $20 per month hydro. All these charges will increase in the next year. There are two children aged seven and four. They eat chicken and hamburger and cannot remember when they had steak or a roast. Of course they cannot afford to go on holidays, and with their income they do not qualify for day-care. They do not go out to eat and only occasionally go to the movies. Fortunately some of their relatives are better off than they and the children get hand-me-down clothes.
Another woman who is a single parent with one son works as a bilingual secretary. Her take home pay is $1,100 per month. She pays $365 per month rent, has no car and takes a bus to work. She has cut back on the kind of food they eat. For them, eating out means going to McDonald's. Her son has finished

high school and would like to go to university but will not be able to unless they get assistance.
These are people who are just getting by, not living high off the hog. This bill means a reduction of 4 to 5 per cent in their real standard of living. I have other examples but I do not want to take the time of the House with them now, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am particularly pleased to take part in the debate on Bill C-124, concerning compensation in the Canadian public sector, because with the member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow),
I believe this is probably the most important bill the House will be considering this session. Mr. Speaker, for forty years we have been working on income redistribution. This has been our principal concern. Our Department of National Health and Welfare, Employment and Immigration, Small Businesses, International Trade, Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Public Works, Agriculture, Energy, Mines and Resources and so on, Mr. Speaker, have been true to this specific concept. Mackenzie King started redistribution for the benefit of senior citizens and children, namely, the old age security pension and family allowances. St. Laurent redistributed income to students through subsidies to the universities. Pearson did the same for sick people when medicare or health insurance was introduced to pay for both medical and hospital expenses. Our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is concerned with redistributing our national wealth in the energy field by trying to Canadianize the industry gradually.
We have done an excellent job of redistribution. In fact, today, we are redistributing $2 billion per month through all these programs. To illustrate what $1 billion represents: If a man gives his wife SI million and asks her to spend $1,000 a day and to come back when she has spent all the money, she would not come back until three years later. If the husband gives his wife $1 billion and asks her to do the same, she would not be heard from for three hundred years. However, Mr. Speaker, with all our concern for redistributing our national wealth, we have tended to neglect the production sector. People forget that in order to spend money, someone has to make it. So, today we have a situation where 1,300,000 Canadians are looking for a job. We have an inflation rate of 12 per cent and our interest rates are absolutely horrendous.
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act

We have to realize, Mr. Speaker, that inflation is at the root of our problems. Inflation is draining the savings of all Canadians, and if we let it go on as it is going today, our so-called middle class will be no more. It is making destitute those Canadians who are on fixed incomes. It is chasing away investors from this country. It is producing high interest rates and pricing Canadian manufacturers and their products out of both local and export markets.
We must defeat inflation, we have no other choice. How do we do this? Our economists have as many solutions as there are economists, but they do have a number of solutions for us. The government has to start somewhere. We know that there are 1.3 million unemployed today, but we sometimes forget there are also nine million Canadians who are employed and worried about their jobs. What we are doing in this bill is asking those nine million Canadians first to help themselves by protecting their own jobs, and second, to help their fellow Canadians who are seeking to regain their jobs. This is what Bill C-124 does. It sets an example, it leads the way.
One of the things mentioned today by the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose) was that there would be no possibility to rectify alleged discriminatory employment practices given the way in which the provisions of Bill C-124 have been formulated. I would like to remind the hon. member that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) has already stated in the House that it is not his intention to have the bill override the equal pay for work of equal value provisions of the Human Rights Act. The enactment of Bill C-124 will not prevent federal public service employees, or any other employee falling under the jurisdiction of the Human Rights Act, from filing "equal pay for work of equal value" complaints with the Canadian Human Rights Commission. It is quite obviously the intention of the government that alleged pay complaints under that act will be handled in the same way they have been since the act was proclaimed in 1978. Any inequities found to exist will be rectified.
To say that Bill C-124 consists of an attack on labour is a very shortsighted view. One cannot deny that a large wage increase would have been better received by our federal employees, but the federal government has not adopted this approach because it fully realizes, as I believe the majority of Canadians in their hearts realize, that, as Carl Beigie of the C.D. Howe Institute, put it: "short-term sacrifices are the only way to beat inflation." There will be a pay-off, he says, if Canadians accept 6 per cent wage increases. He says that "it will provide the necessary adjustments so that inflation will come down, interest rates will fall, and the Canadian dollar will strengthen."
Everyone has to co-operate, Mr. Speaker, and I am confident that everyone will. There is no other choice. Clearly this is not a public relations ploy, as is suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). In response to CLC

Mr. Speaker, I posed my question to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) last Thursday, at which time I asked that an independent person be appointed by the minister to look at all aspects of the herring fishery in the Bay of Fundy. It is kind of odd that at this late date, when the fishery should be well under way, both fishermen and processors have not reached a negotiated price. I say this knowing full well that the parties have been negotiating. I also know that the size of the fish and the red feed in the fish have meant that perhaps it has not been worth while for the plants to be processing them.
We have a quota and we have fishermen to catch it. We have capacity within the plants to process all the quota, yet at this late date we do not have a price for which fishermen feel they can go out and fish. I say this because 1 know that this same group of fishermen went to the Fisheries Prices Support Board last year in order to obtain assistance for last year's herring fishery. They were told to wait and see until the end of this season and until the Kirby commission made its report. We are entering a second year, and at the price of $143 per metric ton, the price to which fishermen have come down from $165, they do not feel they can meet their expenses. The processors are at $120 per metric ton. Plant workers are not working. Fishermen, the captains and their crews, are not working. The owners of the plants say that they have markets which they can fill.
What is the solution? I indicated to the minister that I feel very strongly that somewhere in the system all parties in the fishing industry should know what the prices are on world markets. There should be a system whereby we know what our fish will bring as a return. I have pressed this, and I feel very strongly that the marketing system within the Department of Fisheries and at the provincial level-and I speak mainly as far as Nova Scotia goes-are not being realistic and are not taking an active part.
We had a good example of a plant which opened last year to process herring sardines. It was an A-l product; there were no complaints about it, but market conditions forced the plant to close a year later, after having spent $6 million to open and to acquire a good work force. Here we are without that plant working. No one would have expected that product to have
found a place on the market shelf within one season of operation, yet when it came time for finding the money to operate the plant and to keep the 100 or more people employed in the area, there was no assistance for the plant and it had to go into bankruptcy. There does not appear to be anyone in the system who wants to open it and operate it at the height of the herring season which is upon us.
This just strengthens my position here tonight. We have both fishermen and processors in the Bay of Fundy who are not able to sit down and say that so many tonnes of herring will bring a return on the market and therefore fishermen should get "X" amount. The plants are saying one thing, the fishermen are saying another, but there is no system whereby one can verify against the other. It necessitates an over-the-side sales to help alleviate the problem.
There are many criticisms about over-the-side sales. This year in particular big companies in Nova Scotia are using them to send groundfish into the Portuguese market. We had these in herring in the Bay of Fundy last year. We have them in mackerel in some areas and we have them in Newfoundland with the oversupply of fish being caught there.
We are not directing ourselves to the importance of establishing a market for that 200-mile limit.
I have repeated the fact for many years that we must direct our marketing system to the capacity that exists, the capacity of the fishermen to catch all that is in the 200-mile limit, and the capacity of our plants to process it. We need an effective marketing strategy which requires the processors and the fishermen to know where that market is and what the returns will be in order to make an operation viable. Without that knowledge, we have the situation which presently exists, where fishermen cannot operate without incurring a direct loss at $120 a metric ton, or about $30,000 per boat for this year. It does not pay them to go out and fish. This relates to individual boats and there are many captains who are in that position. There are plant workers as well who would normally be working but are not.
What is the solution? Can we get an extra quota? The biologists say there is no surplus, and they have promised the fishermen that they would go down to verify if that is not the case. Everyone in the area knows that there is a mixed class of fish, of herring, which shows the strength of those stocks, but there are no biologists on those boats. We are entering the height of the season.
Perhaps the solution is to give them an extra quota. Perhaps another solution could be found through the Fisheries Prices Support Board. If this is the solution I believe the companies must open their books to show what they receive on the market for their fish.
I realize that my time is up. I appreciate being allowed to speak as this is a very critical situation which repeats itself every year.
July 12, 1982

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-AUTHORITY FOR CAPPING INDEXATION OF PENSIONS. (B) FUNDING OF INDEXING
PUBLIC SERVICE-AUTHORITY FOR CAPPING INDEXATION OF PENSIONS. (B) FUNDING OF INDEXING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the national energy policy of this government started the economy of Canada on a tailspin. The November 12, 1981, budget accentuated the downward whirl. The June 28, 1982, budget braked the fall a little. But the $20 billion deficit and other items aimed this ailing Canada right at the rocks of disaster.
One of the other items that accentuated the spin was the announcement that the government intended to cap the indexation of the pensions of retired civil servants, retired army personnel and retired RCMP. It is to this doublecross policy which I address my remarks tonight.
During service to the public, these men and women were required to contribute 6.5 per cent of their salaries and wages to the basic pension fund, plus 1 per cent for the purpose of indexing their pensions in periods of inflation.
Adjournment Debate
The minister, in a weak attempt to justify this confiscation of part of the whole pension, said, "the pension of most retired persons from the private sector are not indexed at all". The minister should know that in the private sector, where there is no indexing, the employees were not required to pay into an indexation fund to provide for indexing. If they did pay into a fund for indexing, the company would not dare to cap the indexation after the employee retired, but such honour is foreign to the government. When asked what authority the government had to cap the indexing of these pensions, the minister said, "Authority will be sought from Parliament by way of legislation." Authority will be sought, indeed, when he knows that the trained seals of Mr. Trudeau, the Liberal backbenchers, will vote as they are told.
When I mentioned cutting off part of the pension of the retired, the minister misled the people by saying, "There is no intention to affect the pension rights of the retired." Who does the minister think he is kidding with such misleading predaci-ty? It is certainly not the retired RCMP who have risked their lives many times during their years of service to earn their pension. It is certainly not the handicapped who need every cent of indexing to exist, let alone live, and not the Armed Forces personnel who left part of their lives in the battlefields. The minister well knows that the retired depend on the basic pension plus the indexation which is, in fact, part and parcel of the pension when inflation exists.
When the Progressive Conservative member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Clarke) spoke feelingly on behalf of needy working mothers, the Hon. Mr. MacEachen inferred that incomes of less than $30,000 were "fully protected". Is that not interesting? Let us look at the incomes of these retired army personnel, RCMP and civil servants. Are they in the $30,000 bracket or higher? The average pension of the 119,670 superannuated civil servants, the 30,000 retired soldiers, sailors and air personnel, and the 5,000 RCMP, is $7,915, and their spouses average only $2,100 per year, averages which indicate that many average incomes are under $7,900. The poverty line is generally below $8,000 per year. Here the government is capping indexations on persons living under the poverty line.
Another point is that the moneys contributed to the retirement funds do not belong to the government. They belong to the contributors. All these items did not deter the federal government from capping the indexing of pensions of this group. In effect, the government said, "They are retired; they have no unions; their working days are over. We do not need them any more. To hell with them!" So, in spite of their contributions, in spite of the work they have done, the retirement index of their pension is capped.
"I weep for Canada", one of the superannuates cried. "Do not weep for Canada", I said, "weep for Mr. Trudeau, Mr. Lalonde, Mr. MacEachen and the Liberal government"-

July 12, 1982
Adjournment Debate

Mr. Speaker, it is a real pleasure for me to have stayed tonight until this late hour to listen to the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), who is one of my favourite Members of Parliament. I find on many occasions that even if his facts are thin, his rhetoric is great and fascinating. Tonight is one of those nights.
I find, for example, he is playing the old divide and conquer game again. He tells people that the government's attack against inflation is not going to work and, therefore, they will suffer. That is what he has done tonight, he thinks, on behalf of retired public servants. Fortunately, those people do not accept the line of thought which the hon. member has put forward. For evidence, I refer him to the Ottawa Citizen of June 3, page 71, where that newspaper diligently sought out the opinions of quite a few senior public servants, retired people here in Ottawa. They told that reporter they did not agree with the line of thought being put forward by the hon. member.
I ask the hon. member to remember a simple set of facts, namely that indexed pensions for public servants have only
been in effect since 1970 at a rate of one half per cent of salary and since 1977 at the rate of 1 per cent of salary. Therefore, we are not talking here about contributions that have been made throughout some 40 or 50 years of service, as the hon. member implies.
Finally, I ask him to remember the basic principle that if everyone shoots for 6 per cent, there will be no sacrifice for anyone. However, if everyone shoots for 12 per cent, the hon. member will be right and there will be some people who will suffer. That is why the government is suggesting that 6 per cent is a reasonable target and that the leadership being shown by the government and its employees and retired employees is vital for the whole economy so that we can all prosper. At 6 per cent we prosper; at 12 per cent we weaken. Therefore, we cannot follow the line of thought implied by my dear friend from Bow River who has been charming but, I hate to say, wrong tonight.

subtopic: AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY-CANADIAN CONTENT IN IMPORTED VEHICLES. (B) CONSEQUENCES OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY-CANADIAN CONTENT IN IMPORTED VEHICLES. (B) CONSEQUENCES OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my comments tonight arise out of questions I posed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) on June 22 last. At that time I was asking for information dealing with the progress that this government was making with respect to the Canadian value added in the automobile industry and with respect to quotas that might be affixed to imported automobiles coming into this country, which now hold 25 per cent of the market. The minister's reply was the standard, usual, eloquent one; please be patient and, if you are patient, good deeds will follow. That answer is no longer adequate or acceptable. Not only have we been patient, but we have watched the automobile industry go into a serious decline to the point where it is now just about beyond recovery.
It might interest hon. members that over two years ago, on April 17, 1980, as recorded at page 94 of Hansard, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said, "our priority is to preserve Canadian jobs and to create more Canadian jobs". The minister went on to say that he was going to have formal consultations with the United States of America dealing with the relevant clauses in the Canada-U.S. trade pact. Those consultations were to include as well the matter of imported automobiles. What a track record that minister has. What a priority he set for himself.
Since then he has presided over the highest period of unemployment in the history of the automobile industry. The minister responds, better than two years after claiming auto industry jobs to be a priority, by telling the House, "I look forward to progress and hope to have announcements in the coming months". In other words, Mr. Speaker, he is giving us exactly the same kind of answer he gave us two years ago. In other words, no progress has been made with respect to changes in that trade pact, or quotas for imports, and we have no comments with respect to Canadian value added.
July 12, 1982

1 would like to spell out one or two of the problems that exist. The first is the long-standing problem with respect to the Canada-U.S. trade pact. The auto pact, now in existence for 17 years, has been a disaster for the Canadian auto parts industry. For the last three years there has been an auto parts deficit with the United States in excess of $4 billion each year.
For example, just today 1 received a letter from the president of an auto parts manufacturer in St. Catharines. He pointed out that one of the big three auto manufacturers has served notice on that company that it was going to shift its parts sourcing of a major item from St. Catharines to Detroit. The St. Catharines business offered a 30 per cent price discount. That same manufacturer in St. Catharines had a merit award, called a preferred supplier award. That award was given because of the quality control in that company. Clearly then, the issue of price, the issue of quality, the issue of historical relationship, meant nothing. That car assembler in Detroit was determined to shift the contract to Detroit. The St. Catharines supplier now stands to lose $12 million in lost sales and this country will lose another 80 to 100 jobs. The president of the St. Catharines industry said clearly and flatly that without Canadian control legislation, without Canadian value added, the automobile industry in this country will go down the drain just as badly and just as quickly as the economics of this country is now going down the drain.
That brings me, then, Mr. Speaker, to the question of Canadian value added. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has said that the Volkswagen agreement was the "harbinger of things to come." He also indicated that public pressure would bring about swift action in this matter. Since that time, there has been much evidence of public pressure on Canadians, who now appreciate that at least one in six jobs in Canada is automobile related.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has taken the position that it is vital to Canada's economic well being that we have an automobile industry. 1 want to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that this is an industry that can take a leading part in getting us out of the doldrums we are in now; getting us out of the recession or the depression we are in. If the minister and this government allow the automobile industry to die on a sea of platitudes, promises and empty rhetoric, then we are in a period of sad decline and depression.
It is time for action in the Canada-U.S. auto parts pact amendments and the Canadian context of Canadian value added to every automobile sold within this country. That time for government action, is now. I leave it to the minister or to his parliamentary secretary to give us a more positive response than that which we have had.

Mr. Speaker, I
Adjournment Debate
must say that when I made my comments earlier about the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) being one of my favourite people in the Conservative Party, 1 had forgotten about the member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid). It is a real pleasure to hear a Conservative talk about building up Canadian industry instead of trying to tear apart some of the nationalization programs, or some of the Canadianization programs, or the support programs that we normally are developing for industries across the country.
The hon. member referred to the arrangement with Volkswagen. It is a very good model for Canadians and for other countries wishing to sell cars in Canada. Undoubtedly, as foreign vehicle producers reach decisions about their investment in Canada, they will be consulting with us on the terms available to them to achieve relief from duty in the same way as Volkswagen has. There currently are cases of this type under discussion, and we hope they can be brought to a successful completion in the months ahead.
Volkswagen operated for some years under a duty remission scheme whereby the duty paid on its imported vehicles was reduced in relation to the value of automotive parts purchased by Volkswagen in Canada for use in its assembly facilities in other countries. Once Volkswagen established an assembly plant in the United States, the company substantially increased its purchases of parts from Canadian independent parts producers, but under the formula of the duty remission program Volkswagen was still paying duty on vehicles it was importing into Canada.
The new arrangement involved the establishment of a parts production facility in Canada to employ almost 500 Canadians and to create increased parts purchases in Canada. These extra purchases will in turn create a further 1,000 new jobs. This will permit Volkswagen to import its vehicles duty free provided it obtains the established levels of Canadian content.
The duty remission program which, it seems, was particularly attractive to Volkswagen, is being used by other offshore vehicle producers. In the highly competitive automotive market in Canada today any savings on costs to an automotive producer must be attractive. The duty remission program reduces the level of duty the importer must pay. In the process it creates activity in the automotive manufacturing sector in Canada. It is not, however, possible to have 100 per cent of the duty payable remitted under this program. If a company, for competitive reasons, wants to reduce the amount of duty to zero, then the Volkswagen model should show it how some arrangement can be worked out to give it a similar opportunity. As I mentioned at the beginning, we hope other companies can be encouraged to bring such deals to successful completion within a few months.
